Decomposing the gap into its constitutive physical channels yields two
concrete engineering artifacts, namely a supported deployment envelope
and an explicit residual mismatch list. The supported deployment
envelope defines the bounded domain within which physical hardware
matches simulation within validated tolerances. For the analytical
drive, this envelope specifies approach velocities below
\(0.25\text{ m/s}\), ambient illumination between \(300\text{ lux}\) and
\(600\text{ lux}\), and total loop latency below \(40\text{ ms}\). The
residual mismatch list itemizes every unclosed difference that remains
outside the training distribution, including the
\(1.5\times 10^{-3}\text{ rad/N}\cdot\text{m}\) drivetrain compliance,
the \(49.5\text{ ms}\) \(P_{99}\) latency tail, and the
\(0.40\text{ N}\) thermal sensor drift. Each entry on the residual list
defines an explicit requirement for runtime monitors and safety filters,
which must detect when physical execution drifts past the boundary where
the simulated policy remains valid.

\section{Fine-Tuning on the Real Machine}\label{sec-training-6-6}

When residual errors resist simulation tuning, fine-tuning directly on
physical hardware appears to be the direct path to closure. Instead of
constructing higher-fidelity friction models or identifying unmodeled
drivetrain dynamics through separate system identification routines,
gradient updates computed from physical rollouts adjust the policy
against the actual mechanics of the deployed machine. Adapting a policy
on the deployed machine closes an observed gap and charges physical
exposure for every sample it takes. The policy adjusts its parameters
against the true compliance of the chassis, the true contact dynamics of
the workpiece, and the actual latency profile of the bus. What makes
this trade exacting is that physical interaction is not free. In a
simulator, sampling states near the boundary of stability costs only
compute cycles. On hardware, every sample expends component life,
stresses mechanical interfaces, and risks driving the machine into
unrecoverable contact states.

\textbf{Real-machine fine-tuning debt} is the compounded operational
cost incurred when updating policy parameters on physical hardware,
where gradient steps solve localized contact errors but consume finite
mechanical fatigue life, induce thermal heating in motor windings, and
risk catastrophic forgetting of pre-verified nominal transit stability.

Consider an analytical example of a direct-drive assembly station
adapting an insertion policy to overcome an unmodeled \(1.5\text{ mm}\)
mounting offset. The policy executes at \(50\text{ Hz}\), corresponding
to a sample period of \(20\text{ ms}\). To adapt its final layer weights
to the contact dynamics of a hardened steel fixture, an on-robot
fine-tuning routine collects \(20{,}000\) interaction steps,
representing \(400\text{ s}\) of active contact and near-contact
operation. Because the policy must explore to improve, stochastic action
perturbations generate unpredictable force transients before low-level
feedback can intervene. If \(1.5\%\) of exploratory steps exceed the
nominal \(15.0\text{ N}\) seating force and strike the fixture at a
contact threshold of \(60.0\text{ N}\) before the torque limiters in the
nervous system clamp the command, the fine-tuning run injects \(300\)
impact shocks into the drivetrain.

In this analytical example, the consequences of those \(300\) impact
events can be calculated directly. At an approach velocity of
\(0.08\text{ m/s}\) with an effective moving mass of \(3.5\text{ kg}\),
each impact dissipates
\(\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 3.5\text{ kg} \times (0.08\text{ m/s})^2 = 1.12\times 10^{-2}\text{ J}\)
directly into the gear teeth and bearings. If the cycloidal drive on the
primary joint is rated for a fatigue threshold of \(5.0\times 10^4\)
shock cycles at that peak load, those seven minutes of policy
exploration consume \(300 / (5.0\times 10^4) = 0.60\%\) of the
mechanical life of the reducer. Thermal accumulation introduces an equal
constraint. High-frequency exploration dither elevates the
root-mean-square current through the motor coils from a nominal
\(1.8\text{ A}\) to \(3.6\text{ A}\). In a winding with an electrical
resistance of \(2.2\ \Omega\), Joule heating increases from
\(I^2 R = (1.8\text{ A})^2 \times 2.2\ \Omega = 7.13\text{ W}\) to
\((3.6\text{ A})^2 \times 2.2\ \Omega = 28.51\text{ W}\), quadrupling
thermal dissipation and bringing the motor core to its
\(80^\circ\text{C}\) thermal derating threshold within \(210\text{ s}\)
unless cooling intervals are budgeted into the training schedule.

Beyond mechanical wear, real-world adaptation undermines the statistical
verification established during pre-deployment testing. In simulation, a
policy can be subjected to \(1.0\times 10^7\) validation episodes across
randomized perturbations, establishing bounded tracking errors and tail
behavior out to \(P_{99.9}\). Once weight updates \(\Delta W\) are
applied on hardware, every statistical claim conditioned on the original
parameter vector \(W_0\) is void. The updated policy may resolve the
steady-state force error against the target fixture, yet the gradient
steps can simultaneously degrade free-space tracking accuracy, lower
phase margins during high-speed transit, or distort response profiles
during emergency stops. Because hardware throughput is bounded by
physical time, the machine cannot execute millions of physical trials to
re-establish those confidence bounds. The adapted policy enters
production with a narrower body of empirical evidence than the simulated
baseline it replaced.

Fine-tuning on the deployed machine therefore converts the policy from a
qualified, frozen software component into an evolving state. In an
engineered system, qualification records depend on strict configuration
control, where the exact binary or parameter hash corresponds to a
documented safety case. When online updates alter policy weights during
operation, that qualification record must be re-opened. The burden of
preventing failure shifts entirely from the learned policy to the
deterministic monitors and safety enforcers residing in the nervous
system. Those monitors must be parameterized to intercept the errors of
the baseline policy as well as the unpredictable intermediate behaviors
generated while the optimizer updates weights against physical feedback.

\section{How Training Choices Go Wrong}\label{sec-training-6-7}

A physical failure in a learned policy is rarely an arbitrary numerical
accident. When an articulated arm drops a workpiece or drives a tool
into a fixture, the command was generated by optimization over a
specific dataset, loss function, and observation space. Because the
mathematical objective selects for behaviors that minimize empirical
loss rather than behaviors that satisfy unstated physical requirements,
each training regime leaves an indelible structural footprint in the
resulting policy. An engineer can predict the failure signature of a
policy before the physical machine is assembled by tracing a
five-element inference chain. That chain begins with the training
exposure, which establishes a learned dependency within the network
weights. When a deployment condition violates that dependency, the
policy produces an observable failure signature in its output commands,
dictating the required detector in the nervous system.

The \textbf{policy vulnerability inference chain} is defined as the
causal five-stage framework
(\(\text{Exposure} \to \text{Dependency} \to \text{Violated Assumption} \to \text{Observable Signature} \to \text{Nervous Interceptor}\))
used to predict hardware destruction modes and synthesize protective
safety monitors before physical machine deployment.

In behavioral cloning, the training exposure consists of state
trajectories recorded under competent human demonstration or a classical
controller. Because competent demonstrators avoid unrecoverable errors,
the training dataset contains zero transitions originating in degraded,
stalled, or off-nominal states. The learned dependency is strict, as the
policy assumes that every input observation resides within the narrow
support of the demonstration distribution. When a mechanical jolt, a
thermal drift in a sensor, or a momentary torque limit shifts the
machine by a tracking error of \(15\text{ mm}\), that deployment
condition violates the distribution boundary. The resulting failure
signature is compounding covariate shift. The policy does not output
mathematical singularities or out-of-bounds numbers. Instead, it emits
continuous, kinematically plausible commands that steer the actuators
into regions of state space where the policy has never received training
signal. Within the brain, the command appears normal. If the nervous
system lacks an explicit distribution monitor or novelty filter at its
input interface, this failure mode cannot be detected until the machine
physically collides with an obstacle or exceeds an envelope limit.

In trial-based learning within simulation, the training exposure
consists of millions of synthetic interactions against a numerical
physics engine. The learned dependency is the set of mathematical
simplifications chosen to keep the simulation fast. When the simulator
models dry friction without velocity-dependent Stribeck curves, assumes
an unvarying communication latency of \(0\text{ ms}\), or calculates
contact forces through instantaneous penalty springs that allow
penetration without restitution, the policy exploits those numerical
artifacts to maximize its reward. During deployment, the machine
encounters real physical dynamics. In an analytical example with an
approach velocity of \(0.5\text{ m/s}\), a transport delay of
\(16\text{ ms}\) across the digital bus means the body travels
\((0.5\text{ m/s}) \times 0.016\text{ s} = 8.0\text{ mm}\) into the
physical boundary before the brain receives the first contact frame and
computes a deceleration command. In the simulator, where latency was set
to \(0\text{ ms}\) and contact was modeled as a soft penalty spring, the
policy learned to decelerate within that \(8.0\text{ mm}\) window
without bouncing. On physical hardware, the unyielding metal contact
stops the tool in less than \(1.0\text{ ms}\), driving transient contact
forces past \(450\text{ N}\) and tripping the actuator overcurrent
protection.\sidenote{\footnotesize Under ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 (Power and Force
  Limiting), transient dynamic impact forces are capped between
  \(140\text{ N}\) and \(210\text{ N}\). Unmodeled simulation contact
  spikes exceeding \(450\text{ N}\) violate these statutory safety
  envelopes, requiring independent physical safety interlocks.} This
failure mode is detectable before deployment by evaluating the policy in
a simulation test environment with injected latency jitter, and at
runtime by tracking force derivatives and high-frequency command chatter
in the nervous system.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-incidentux2a-6.9}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-incident}{Landmark Engineering Incident:}{Tooling Collision from Simulation Contact and Latency Mismatch}
\phantomsection\label{callout-incident*-6.9}

\emph{System:} High-speed robotic pick-and-place assembly cell with
direct-drive Cartesian gantry, six-axis wrist force-torque sensor, and
end-to-end neural motion policy running at \(50\text{ Hz}\) over an
EtherCAT fieldbus.

\emph{Incident:} End-effector tooling collision during automated seating
of a machined aluminum connector, fracturing the precision ceramic
alignment guide, shearing the wrist load-cell mounting pins, and causing
a 6-hour assembly line shutdown.

\emph{Telemetry snapshot:} At \(t = 0.000\text{ s}\), the policy
initiates vertical descent from \(150\text{ mm}\) clearance at
\(v_z = 0.50\text{ m/s}\); at \(t = 0.280\text{ s}\), physical contact
occurs at \(z = 0.0\text{ mm}\); due to a \(16.7\text{ ms}\) camera
exposure time and an \(8.2\text{ ms}\) bus transmission delay, the first
contact frame reaches the policy at \(t = 0.305\text{ s}\)
(\(25\text{ ms}\) late); during this unobserved interval, the gantry
moves \(12.5\text{ mm}\) past the contact plane; at
\(t = 0.308\text{ s}\), peak normal force spikes to \(465\text{ N}\) at
a rate \(dF/dt > 3.8\times 10^4\text{ N/s}\), shearing mechanical load
pins before the drive controller trips on overcurrent at
\(t = 0.312\text{ s}\).

\emph{Root cause:} The rigid-body simulation engine modeled contact
using an idealized compliant penalty spring with zero transport delay,
allowing the policy to learn an unbraked plunge strategy that relied on
immediate synthetic force feedback to arrest momentum.

\emph{Architectural flaw:} Absence of an independent runtime
velocity-envelope governor and hardware force-derivative (\(dF/dt\))
clamp in the nervous system to restrict kinetic energy prior to
touch-down regardless of policy command outputs.

\emph{Provenance:} Precision manufacturing cell automated commissioning
incident log and post-mortem failure analysis report.

\end{fbxSimple}

Training through trial directly on physical hardware eliminates the
simulation gap, but it introduces an opposite structural dependency. The
training exposure consists of unconstrained physical interactions guided
by an engineered scalar reward. The learned dependency is the exact
mathematical formulation of that reward function. Engineers frequently
treat real dynamics as a natural safeguard against unrealistic
behaviors, assuming that physical execution prevents the policy from
finding shortcuts. The machine, however, discovers physically valid
strategies that satisfy the mathematical reward while violating unstated
operational constraints. If the reward function rewards rapid velocity
regulation toward a workpiece and penalizes final position error without
penalizing torque derivatives, the optimizer converges on aggressive
bang-bang control. The observable failure signature is unconstrained
mechanical stress and thermal overload. In an analytical example where a
joint motor with a winding resistance of \(1.5\ \Omega\) switches
between its current limits of \(+12\text{ A}\) and \(-12\text{ A}\) at
\(80\text{ Hz}\), the sustained root-mean-square current produces Joule
heating of
\(I^2 R = (12\text{ A})^2 \times 1.5\ \Omega = 216\text{ W}\), elevating
the stator core temperature past its \(90^\circ\text{C}\) thermal
derating limit within \(180\text{ s}\). The task-level reward monitor
records full success and detects no failure. Detection requires the
nervous system to monitor physical observables that were omitted from
the training reward, including motor coil temperatures, current spectra,
and high-frequency accelerometer energy.

When a base policy is fine-tuned on physical hardware to correct
localized errors, the training exposure is restricted to a narrow task
slice collected over a brief operating window. The learned dependency is
an over-representation of recent local transitions coupled with the
deliberate suppression of dangerous trajectories. When human operators
intervene or safety tripwires halt execution during training, those
intervention states are censored from the update buffer to avoid
reinforcing abort sequences. The observable failure signature is
regression and boundary instability. While the policy improves
steady-state force regulation against a specific production fixture,
gradient updates overwrite the parameter representations that maintained
stability during free-space transit or off-axis approaches. The policy
loses competence on previously verified nominal states, failing when
presented with lighting angles or approach vectors that were common in
the pretraining dataset but absent during the fine-tuning session.
Because the neural network assigns valid output magnitudes across all
inputs, this internal regression is undetectable by the policy itself.
Detecting it requires a pre-deployment regression test suite on frozen
hardware benchmarks to evaluate non-adapted operational modes before the
updated weights are granted authority over physical actuators.

Hybrid pipelines that combine simulation pretraining, demonstration
filtering, and real-world fine-tuning do not eliminate these structural
failure modes. Instead, they shift the dominant failure signature across
the lifecycle. A policy initialized from demonstrations and refined in
simulation shifts its primary risk from covariate drift to simulator
exploitation. When that policy is subsequently fine-tuned on hardware
for contact regulation, the updates suppress simulator exploitation at
the point of contact but induce forgetting in the upstream velocity
approach. The earlier failure mechanisms remain latent within the
network weights, ready to trigger whenever operating conditions push the
machine outside the fine-tuned envelope.

Predicting these signature failures establishes three concrete
engineering obligations for the system designer. First, every identified
training dependency requires a predeployment test obligation, consisting
of a verification test protocol designed to stress the exact boundary
where the training environment deviated from physical reality. Second,
where the physical failure manifests in measurable mechanical
quantities, the nervous system must incorporate a dedicated runtime
detector operating at the loop rate, whether monitoring tracking
deviation, force rate of change, or current spectra. Third, where
detection is physically or mathematically impossible, such as ungrounded
commands caused by covariate shift in pure cloning, the system
specification must declare an explicit unsupported operating envelope
and rely on deterministic safety interlocks to refuse policy authority.
Fulfilling these obligations requires that the engineering team maintain
an exact, immutable record of how the policy was constructed, detailing
the source data, the simulator dynamics, the reward terms, and every
modification applied across its training history.

\section{The Policy Manifest}\label{sec-training-6-8}

The training record establishes the causal link between how a policy was
constructed and how it behaves when granted authority over physical
actuators. Where Chapter~\ref{sec-nervous} defines the base engineering
notebook, including its immutable hashing, schema inheritance, and
versioning rules, this section specifies only the domain fields that
Chapter~\ref{sec-training} adds to that schema. A learned policy does
not fail generically. It fails along the exact seam lines where its
training regime, source demonstrations, or simulation environment
departed from physical reality. Capturing those seam lines requires
logging the sequence of optimization stages, the bounded support of the
training data, the simulator solver parameters, and every hardware
exposure incurred during real-world adaptation.

The \textbf{training provenance record} is defined as the immutable
notebook schema extension that registers optimization stage checkpoints,
empirical demonstration support manifolds, physics engine version
hashes, domain randomization intervals, solver omissions, and hardware
fine-tuning wear logs to predict physical deployment failure modes.

As detailed in the provenance record schema
(Table~\ref{tbl-06-training-schema}), every physical AI training
pipeline executes a sequence of distinct regimes where objectives, data
distributions, and stopping criteria change. The training record
registers each stage in this sequence, beginning with the source
checkpoint hash and detailing the mathematical formulation of the loss
function or reward vector. For each stage, the record documents the
stopping rule, whether governed by an epoch count, a validation loss
threshold, or a plateau in simulated return, alongside the engineering
rationale for advancing to the next regime. In an analytical example
where a manipulator is trained to approach a surface at
\(1.2\text{ m/s}\) and regulate contact force to \(8.0\text{ N}\),
pretraining on kinesthetic demonstrations might be terminated after
\(500\) epochs to prevent overfitting to a single human demonstrator. If
training then transitions to reinforcement learning in simulation to
expand angular coverage, the record logs that motivation and references
the exact initial weights ingested by the simulator. Without this stage
provenance, an engineer diagnosing an unstable velocity profile cannot
determine whether oscillations originated in the demonstration weights
or were introduced during subsequent simulation updates.

For every dataset ingested during imitation or offline optimization, the
record specifies the dataset version identifier, the data collection
policy, the environmental operating conditions, and the source of the
control commands. It records whether trajectories were generated by an
expert scripted controller, a human teleoperator, or rollouts from an
earlier policy checkpoint, alongside sensor calibration matrices and
physical workspace parameters present during logging. The record
explicitly quantifies the state-action support over which demonstrations
actually exist. If human demonstrations of a surface-wiping task contain
end-effector velocities between \(0.2\text{ m/s}\) and
\(0.8\text{ m/s}\) and contact angles within \(10^\circ\) of the surface
normal, the record marks the boundary of that support manifold. When the
deployed policy is presented with an approach angle of \(25^\circ\), the
record reveals that the network is operating on ungrounded extrapolation
rather than demonstrated competence.

Standard machine learning pipelines frequently discard aborted episodes,
operator vetoes, and safety interlock interventions to prevent
sub-optimal actions from entering the training loss. In physical
systems, filtering out these events discards the exact evidence needed
to identify where the policy required assistance. The training record
preserves every intervention, emergency stop assertion, and truncated
trajectory as structured negative metadata. If a human supervisor
intervened eighteen times across two hundred trial runs to prevent a
tool from striking an alignment fixture during touchdown, recording the
joint positions, velocities, and motor current spikes at the moment of
each override exposes the state space region where the policy lost
tracking stability. Retaining these aborted trajectories ensures the
ledger reflects the true failure boundaries encountered during training
rather than a curated subset of successful rollouts.

When policy weights are optimized in simulation, the training record
captures the physics engine build hash, the interface contract between
the policy and the simulator, the reward formulation, the numerical
integration method, and the solver timestep, such as a fixed
\(2.0\text{ ms}\) step at \(500\text{ Hz}\). It documents the domain
randomization distributions applied to link masses, surface friction
coefficients, actuator response latencies, and sensor noise profiles.
The record also logs known physical omissions, identifying the unmodeled
dynamics that were deliberately excluded from the simulation graph to
maintain training throughput. If a rigid-body simulator omits harmonic
drive compliance, structural deflection under a \(5.0\text{ kg}\)
payload, or thermal resistance changes in motor windings, the record
lists those omissions as unverified dynamic assumptions. When the
resulting policy exhibits limit-cycle oscillations during high-load
contact on the physical bench, the omission log directs the diagnosis
directly to joint compliance rather than ungrounded parameter drift.

Real-machine adaptation introduces mechanical wear and localized
parameter shifts that must be tracked across the hardware lifecycle. The
training record registers the hardware serial numbers, physical
configurations, and calibration offsets of the adaptation test bench,
along with the cumulative physical exposure measured in runtime hours,
contact cycles, or total work performed. It lists the exact parameter
subset modified during adaptation, distinguishing between full weight
updates, adapter layer tuning, and output-head fine-tuning, while
logging every anomaly or actuator limit reached during the session.
After adaptation updates are computed, the record captures the execution
results of a frozen regression test suite. If adapting a policy to
soften touchdown impact on a rigid surface increases tracking error
during the preceding free-space transit by \(14\text{ mm}\), the
regression ledger records that loss of nominal capability before the
modified weights are granted authority over physical actuators.

The training record separates empirical optimization results from the
declared operating envelope of the machine. High training reward or low
loss on an offline split does not demonstrate that the policy is safe to
execute across all environmental states. The record defines the claimed
operating envelope across payload masses, approach velocities, thermal
bounds, and surface geometries, while maintaining a separate ledger of
unobserved, excluded, or weakly supported conditions. If training data
includes surface approaches only under ambient illumination between
\(200\text{ lx}\) and \(500\text{ lx}\) with rigid flat workpieces, the
record declares curved surfaces, compliant substrates, and illumination
levels below \(100\text{ lx}\) as unsupported operational modes. This
separation prevents a convergent training metric from being mistaken for
an operational clearance across uncharacterized physical regimes.

Downstream engineering teams consume the training record throughout the
design, evaluation, and release lifecycle. Chapter~\ref{sec-evaluation}
uses the recorded support boundaries and simulation omissions to
construct targeted empirical evaluation suites that probe the specific
failure modes predicted by each training regime. Runtime safety monitors
and deterministic enforcement layers in Chapter~\ref{sec-enforcement}
use the recorded data support bounds to parameterize out-of-distribution
detectors and determine when policy authority must be curtailed.
Verification frameworks in Chapter~\ref{sec-verification} and the
multi-layer safety case in Chapter~\ref{sec-release} draw on the record
to establish the provenance of every parameter update and verify that
known simulation omissions are bounded by independent physical
interlocks. Maintaining this complete record ensures that when a policy
achieves high scores across its training benchmarks, engineers do not
mistake optimization convergence for physical reliability.

\section{Systems Stress-Tests}\label{sec-training-6-9}

A policy that is better by every training metric can be worse on the
physical machine. In physical systems, minimizing empirical loss across
an offline demonstration split or maximizing return inside a numerical
simulator evaluates compliance with the training environment rather than
competence on physical hardware. When an optimization objective rewards
behaviors that exploit data curation filters or simulator
approximations, the ranking of candidate policies established during
training inverts upon deployment. Evaluating a trained policy before
granting it authority over actuators requires stress-testing the causal
assumptions that connect training metrics to physical outcomes.

\begin{figure}[t]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{index_files/mediabag//Users/VJ/GitHub/MLSysBook-integrate-physical/physical/book/chapters/06-training/figures/fig06_policy_ranking_inversion.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-06-policy-ranking-inversion}\textbf{Policy
Performance Ranking Inversion across Training and Physical Hardware
Outcomes.} Three analytical case studies demonstrating how optimization
gains in training invert upon closed-loop physical deployment. (1) Flow
Regulation: Sanitizing 50 operator recovery runs lowers validation loss
\(4\times\) (\(0.042\text{ V}^2 \to 0.011\text{ V}^2\)), but collapses
physical closed-loop recovery (\(100\% \to 0\%\)) when a supply pressure
drop occurs. (2) Surface Touchdown: An unbraked plunge achieves \(28\%\)
higher simulated return by exploiting soft penalty interpenetration, but
shatters physical load-cell flexures (\(68.0\text{ N}\) peak force
vs.~\(11.4\text{ N}\) for the braked baseline). (3) Regime Transition:
Replacing behavioral cloning with simulation RL achieves \(100\%\)
simulated task success, but commands \(65\text{ Hz}\) high-frequency
torque chatter that excites mechanical resonance, trips motor winding
thermal protection (\(95^\circ\text{C}\)), and reduces hardware
completion to \(12\%\).}

\end{figure}%

The following three analytical stress-tests evaluate machines that
regulate motion and touch surfaces, demonstrating how nominal training
gains convert into physical failure modes:

\subsection*{Stress-Test 1: Recovery Curation and Policy Reversal in
Flow Regulation (State Support
Truncation)}\label{stress-test-1-recovery-curation-and-policy-reversal-in-flow-regulation-state-support-truncation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 1: Recovery Curation and
Policy Reversal in Flow Regulation (State Support Truncation)}

\emph{The scenario.} Two behavioral-cloning policies are trained to
regulate fluid flow via a proportional valve at \(50\text{ Hz}\).
Dataset A contains 500 demonstrated runs including 50 recovery maneuvers
where an operator corrected for transient supply pressure drops to
\(120\text{ kPa}\). Dataset B filters out the 50 recovery runs to
maximize smoothness, retaining 450 nominal runs near \(200\text{ kPa}\).
Policy A achieves an offline validation loss of
\(\text{MSE} = 0.042\text{ (V)}^2\) across the full distribution, while
Policy B achieves \(\text{MSE} = 0.011\text{ (V)}^2\) on its held-out
split, appearing nearly four times more accurate.

\emph{The systems dilemma.} Under a physical supply pressure transient
dropping to \(130\text{ kPa}\), Policy A restores nominal flow within
\(140\text{ ms}\) (\(\Delta P = 15\text{ kPa}\)). Policy B enters an
unrecoverable diverging oscillation that breaches the reservoir overflow
limit within \(800\text{ ms}\). Sanitizing recovery episodes
artificially lowers offline validation error by eliminating
high-variance, multi-modal demonstration segments, blinding the policy
to the off-nominal states its own compounding errors will generate.

\emph{The systems verdict: State Support Invariant.} Offline validation
error measures agreement with recorded history rather than closed-loop
stability. Pruning recovery trajectories improves the training score
while removing the negative feedback manifold required to survive
physical disturbances.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 2: Contact Model Exploitation in Surface
Touchdown (The Simulation Energy
Sink)}\label{stress-test-2-contact-model-exploitation-in-surface-touchdown-the-simulation-energy-sink}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 2: Contact Model
Exploitation in Surface Touchdown (The Simulation Energy Sink)}

\emph{The scenario.} A direct-drive vertical actuator
(\(m = 2.5\text{ kg}\)) approaches a rigid fixture at
\(0.40\text{ m/s}\) to establish a steady normal force
\(F_N = 10.0\text{ N}\). In simulation, Policy 2 achieves \(28\%\)
higher return than Policy 1, reaching target force in \(12\text{ ms}\)
(versus \(45\text{ ms}\) for Policy 1) by plunging into the surface at
\(0.35\text{ m/s}\), exploiting an idealized linear spring-damper
contact solver that arrests momentum in a single integration step
(\(2.0\text{ ms}\)).

\emph{The systems dilemma.} On physical hardware, structural compliance
(\(k = 8.0\times 10^4\text{ N/m}\)) and \(12\text{ ms}\) sensory lag
prevent instantaneous force generation. When Policy 2 strikes the
surface at \(0.35\text{ m/s}\), physical contact force spikes to
\(68.0\text{ N}\) before the first sensor measurement arrives,
shattering the load-cell flexure. Policy 1 decelerates to
\(0.06\text{ m/s}\) prior to touchdown, seating safely in
\(52\text{ ms}\) with a peak force of \(11.4\text{ N}\).

\emph{The systems verdict: Simulator Exploitation Law.} Optimization
algorithms treat simulator simplifications as physical affordances. When
a numerical contact solver permits instantaneous momentum transfer,
learned policies develop high-velocity impact strategies that destroy
physical hardware.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 3: Failure Migration across Regime Transitions
(Data Debt vs Modeling
Debt)}\label{stress-test-3-failure-migration-across-regime-transitions-data-debt-vs-modeling-debt}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 3: Failure Migration
across Regime Transitions (Data Debt vs Modeling Debt)}

\emph{The scenario.} An assembly arm executes a \(200\text{ mm}\)
free-space transit at \(v = 0.50\text{ m/s}\) before preloading a gasket
to \(12.0\text{ N}\). Behavioral cloning (Policy A) exhibits \(34\%\)
task failure due to compounding lateral drift. Replacing cloning with
rigid-body reinforcement learning in simulation (Policy B) achieves
\(100\%\) simulated success and eliminates free-space drift across 100
physical trials.

\emph{The systems dilemma.} To seat the seal rapidly, Policy B learned
in simulation to apply high-frequency torque chatter at
\(65\text{ Hz}\), exploiting the simulator's massless rotor assumption.
On hardware, \(65\text{ Hz}\) chatter excites drivetrain resonance,
heating motor windings from \(28^{\circ}\text{C}\) to the
\(95^{\circ}\text{C}\) thermal limit in \(45\text{ s}\) and collapsing
physical completion rate to \(12\%\).

\emph{The systems verdict: Failure Migration Law.} Changing a training
regime does not eliminate engineering debt; it converts one failure
currency into another. Shifting from human demonstrations to simulation
replaces data-support limits with unmodeled physical dynamics limits.

\section{Summary}\label{sec-training-6-10}

Behavioral cloning purchases operational capability at minimal compute
cost by mapping recorded sensory observations directly to demonstrated
actions. It bypasses the combinatorial complexity of reward design and
avoids running dangerous trial trajectories on physical mechanisms. The
cost of this simplicity is an absolute dependence on the state-space
support of the demonstration dataset. Because the training objective
penalizes deviations only along demonstrated paths, the resulting policy
learns nothing about states outside that narrow manifold. When an
external disturbance, a worn bearing, or a dropped camera frame pushes
the machine into an unrecorded configuration, the policy encounters
covariate shift. In these unrepresented states, the network emits
ungrounded actuator commands with high numerical confidence, compounding
the tracking error with each control cycle until the physical system
collides with an obstacle or exceeds a joint limit.

Trial-based reinforcement learning purchases closed-loop recovery
experience. By exposing the agent to errors during training, it produces
policies that actively correct perturbations and steer the mechanism
back toward the task manifold when disturbances occur. This resilience
is paid for through mechanical wear, clock time, exploration risk, and
reward specification debt. On physical hardware, accumulating the
millions of transitions required for policy convergence subjects
gearboxes, ball screws, and motor windings to repetitive mechanical and
thermal stress. Every exploration step risks driving an end-effector
into a hard fixture or drawing stall current long enough to trip a
thermal breaker. When developers construct a scalar reward function to
guide this search, any misalignment between the mathematical objective
and the physical design intent invites policy exploitation, producing
aggressive, chatter-inducing torque profiles that satisfy the numerical
metric while destroying the physical transmission.

Simulation decouples experience generation from the constraints of
real-time physics and mechanical wear, allowing billions of synthetic
transitions to accumulate across parallel compute clusters at zero
hardware risk. What simulation delivers in throughput, it charges in
modeling debt. Every physics engine represents a versioned mathematical
compromise containing an explicit set of modeled kinematic links, an
explicit set of omitted physical phenomena, and a collection of
numerical approximations. Effects such as motor back-electromotive
force, rotor inertia, contact friction hysteresis, structural
compliance, and sensor thermal noise are routinely simplified or
neglected to sustain high simulation frame rates. The learned policy
optimizes against the exact numerical artifact presented by the solver.
If the simulator treats a joint as a zero-inertia actuator capable of
instantaneous torque reversal, the policy will exploit that unphysical
affordance, leaving the machine vulnerable to resonance, motor
overheating, and mechanical failure when transferred to real hardware.

Physical fine-tuning attempts to reconcile these discrepancies by taking
gradient steps on small batches of rollouts collected directly on the
machine. This step can resolve local tracking errors, adjust for
unmodeled contact compliance at an assembly jig, or tune gain responses
to match physical surface friction. Yet localized fine-tuning carries
its own systemic tax. Updating network weights against a narrow
distribution of hardware rollouts risks eroding the broad recovery
behaviors acquired during large-scale pretraining or simulation.
Overwriting parameters to solve a specific contact mismatch can compress
the effective support of the policy, inducing catastrophic forgetting
across unvisited regions of the state space and degrading the machine's
ability to handle nominal kinematic variations or payload changes.

The durable output of the training process is therefore not simply a
binary weights file, but the complete training record. This artifact
defines the physical and operational boundaries of the learned policy by
recording its provenance. For cloned models, the training record
documents the demonstrated state-space envelope, operator skill
variance, and sensor calibration baselines. For trial-based and
simulated models, it documents the reward formulations, exploration
boundaries, simulator version identifiers, integrator time-steps,
contact solver tolerances, and explicitly unmodeled physical effects.
Without this provenance, a systems engineer cannot predict the failure
modes of the policy, budget appropriate thermal and current margins in
the nervous system, or construct meaningful stress tests to probe the
boundaries of safe authority.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-takeawaysux2a-6.10}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-takeaways}{Key Chapter Takeaways}{}
\phantomsection\label{callout-takeaways*-6.10}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Optimization Inversion (Good in Training, Bad on Hardware):}
  Offline loss minimization and simulated return evaluate numerical
  compliance rather than physical stability. Policies that score highest
  on sanitized datasets often fail catastrophic first-contact trials due
  to unmodeled contact compliance or omitted rotor inertia.
\item
  \textbf{Behavioral Cloning Compounds Off-Support Drift:} Supervised
  imitation penalizes deviations only along demonstrated trajectories.
  Small tracking errors push the body into unvisited states where the
  policy emits ungrounded high-confidence commands, requiring continuous
  \(\mathcal{C}^2\) action chunking or recovery demonstrations.
\item
  \textbf{Simulators Charge Modeling Debt for Scaled Throughput:}
  Physics engines accelerate throughput by simplifying contact friction
  hysteresis, motor back-EMF, and structural compliance. Learned
  policies aggressively exploit these numerical simplifications,
  commanding unphysical torque chatter that overheats real actuators.
\item
  \textbf{Hardware Fine-Tuning Risks Catastrophic Forgetting:} Taking
  gradient steps on narrow physical hardware batches can fix local
  contact errors while silently destroying global recovery manifolds and
  inflating tracking error across nominal transit regimes.
\item
  \textbf{The Training Record is the True Engineering Output:} A
  checkpoint file without provenance is an uncharacterizable liability.
  Dependable physical AI requires an immutable training record detailing
  dataset support boundaries, simulator solver assumptions, and declared
  operational envelopes.
\end{itemize}

\end{fbxSimple}

Chapter~\ref{sec-evaluation} receives this policy alongside its
inherited modeling assumptions, unrepresented state volumes, and
actuator demands. A training record documenting zero regression loss, a
simulated success rate of \(100\%\), or a high cumulative reward in a
software sandbox establishes only that the optimization algorithm
converged under its training conditions. It does not establish that the
policy will move real mass without exceeding motor thermal limits,
violating timing deadlines, or causing mechanical damage. Proving
whether the learned policy can be trusted with physical authority
requires empirical evaluation on hardware under strict physical and
temporal constraints, testing the machine against the very failures that
its training regime chose to defer.

\chapter{\texorpdfstring{Closed-Loop
Evaluation\chaptersubtitle{What Can Be Established About a Policy, and What Cannot}}{Closed-Loop Evaluation}}\label{sec-evaluation}

\begin{figure}[H]

\centering{

\includegraphics[width=1\linewidth,height=\textheight,keepaspectratio]{index_files/mediabag//Users/VJ/GitHub/MLSysBook-integrate-physical/physical/book/chapters/07-evaluation/figures/fig_locator.pdf}

}

\caption{\label{fig-locator}\textbf{Systems Organ Focus: Brain.} Exact
one-sided \(95\%\) lower confidence bounds on true success probability
as a function of zero-failure physical trial count \(n\), illustrating
how statistical confidence scales from \(86.1\%\) at \(n=20\) to
\(99.9\%\) at \(n=2{,}995\) and exposing the wide tail risk that remains
under small testing budgets.}

\end{figure}%

\emph{Why does passing twenty consecutive physical trials without
failure tell you surprisingly little about whether the machine is safe
to deploy?}

Standard machine learning workflows evaluate models by measuring average
accuracy or loss across static, held-out test splits. In physical
systems, open-loop prediction metrics are almost completely uncorrelated
with closed-loop survival. A policy with negligible offline tracking
error can diverge catastrophically in physical execution because its own
actions shift the observation stream into unfamiliar territory. Physical
AI demands closed-loop evaluation methodologies grounded in
non-asymptotic statistics and extreme-value tail analysis. Verifying an
embodied agent requires measuring performance across worst-case
operating envelope boundaries, calculating exact Clopper-Pearson
binomial coverage bounds (\(86.1\%\) at \(n=20\)), and enforcing
pre-registered stopping oracles to expose heavy-tailed physical risks.

\newpage{}

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-objectiveux2a-7.1}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-objective}{Learning Objectives}{}
\phantomsection\label{callout-objective*-7.1}

After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  State what a success rate on \(N\) physical trials actually supports,
  with its exact non-asymptotic confidence interval.
\item
  Explain why an open-loop dataset metric misleads in a specific,
  predictable direction in closed-loop physical execution.
\item
  Compute the exact physical trial count and wall-clock testing budget
  required to certify a target reliability claim under zero failures.
\item
  Apply Extreme Value Theory (EVT) and the Butler \& Finelli
  infeasibility bound to identify physical tail hazards that empirical
  hours cannot cover.
\item
  Construct an immutable physical evaluation record and formalize a
  pre-registered stopping oracle to prevent benchmark gaming and
  censored trial fallacies.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Core chapter takeaway.} No pre-deployment evaluation can establish
deployment behavior, because the policy determines the distribution it
will meet. And twenty clean trials support a far weaker claim than the
number feels like it does.

\end{fbxSimple}

\section{Closed-Loop Survival}\label{sec-evaluation-7-1}

\lettrine{A}{s mapped}\lettrine{i}{n} the systems architecture locator
(Figure~\ref{fig-locator}), the evaluation framework sits within the
Brain organ, establishing what can and cannot be mathematically and
empirically established about a learned policy before granting it
authority over physical actuators. Consider an autonomous mobile robot
that completes twenty consecutive navigation runs across a test
facility, traveling at \(1.5\text{ m/s}\) along a cluttered corridor
without striking a wall or requiring human intervention. In a robotics
laboratory, that result is frequently celebrated as a perfect
demonstration: twenty out of twenty runs passed, yielding an observed
empirical success rate of \(\hat{p} = 100\%\). In classical machine
learning, where held-out test splits contain thousands of static images,
an empirical score of \(100\%\) suggests near-perfection. In a physical
machine, that conclusion is an illusion created by small-sample
statistics.

To determine what twenty clean trials actually prove, we model the
sequence of physical trials as independent and identically distributed
Bernoulli experiments governed by an unknown true operational success
probability \(p\). As derived in the margin, setting the binomial
likelihood of twenty consecutive successes equal to our statistical
significance threshold (\(\alpha = 0.05\)) reveals that the minimum
success probability that would produce twenty clean runs at least
\(5\%\) of the time is only \(86.1\%\). This calculation---the exact
Clopper-Pearson lower bound---reveals the stark evidentiary deficit of
small testing budgets.\sidenote{\footnotesize For zero-failure testing, standard Wald
  confidence intervals degenerate to zero width. The exact
  Clopper-Pearson interval yields
  \(p_{\text{upper}} = 1 - \alpha^{1/n}\), preventing asymptotic
  Gaussian approximations from understating catastrophic risk in
  rare-event tail distributions.} If the true operational reliability of
the vehicle were \(86.1\%\), the probability of observing twenty
straight successes would be exactly \(5\%\). If the true reliability
were below \(86.1\%\), the probability of observing twenty clean runs
would fall below \(5\%\), allowing us to reject the hypothesis
\(p < 0.861\) at the \(95\%\) confidence level.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-definitionux2a-7.2}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-definition}{Definition:}{Clopper-Pearson Non-Asymptotic Bound}
\phantomsection\label{callout-definition*-7.2}

The \textbf{Clopper-Pearson non-asymptotic bound} is an exact
statistical lower confidence limit on true operational success
probability derived from the inverted cumulative binomial distribution
(evaluating to \(p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n}\) for zero failures
across \(n\) independent trials at confidence level \(1-\alpha\)),
establishing the mathematical ceiling of empirical testing without
assuming asymptotic normality.

\end{fbxSimple}

Crucially, twenty successes in twenty trials does not prove that the
robot is \(100\%\) reliable, nor even \(95\%\) reliable. It proves only
that the true success probability is at least \(86.1\%\) at \(95\%\)
confidence. A physical system that fails once in every eight attempts
(\(p = 87.5\%\)) will successfully complete twenty consecutive test runs
more than \(6.9\%\) of the time (\(0.875^{20} \approx 0.0692\)). A
flawless score in twenty runs is entirely consistent with a physical
machine that suffers a catastrophic boundary violation nearly once every
seven deployments.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-ruleux2a-7.3}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-rule}{Architect’s Rule of Thumb:}{Twenty Clean Runs}
\phantomsection\label{callout-rule*-7.3}

Twenty consecutive successes in a laboratory test cell establish an
\(86.1\%\) lower confidence bound, not a \(100\%\) reliability
certificate. A flawless score in twenty runs is mathematically
consistent with a physical system that fails once in every seven
deployments.

\end{fbxSimple}

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-mathux2a-7.4}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-math}{Fermi Math:}{Derivation of the 20-Run Lower Bound}
\phantomsection\label{callout-math*-7.4}

\emph{Problem:} An autonomous robot completes \(n = 20\) physical
navigation runs with zero collisions or human interventions
(\(k = 20\)). What is the exact one-sided \(95\%\) lower confidence
bound on its true operational success probability \(p\)?

\emph{Mathematical Derivation:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Under independent Bernoulli trials, the probability of \(n\)
  consecutive successes is \(P(k = n) = p^n\).
\item
  To find the lower bound \(p_{\text{lower}}\) at confidence level
  \(1 - \alpha = 0.95\) (\(\alpha = 0.05\)), solve:
  \[p_{\text{lower}}^n = \alpha \implies p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n}\]
\item
  Substitute \(n = 20\) and \(\alpha = 0.05\):
  \[\ln(p_{\text{lower}}) = \frac{\ln(0.05)}{20} = \frac{-2.99573}{20} = -0.149787\]
  \[p_{\text{lower}} = e^{-0.149787} \approx 0.86089 \implies 86.09\%\]
\item
  \emph{Implied Maximum Failure Risk:}
  \[\text{Failure Probability} \le 1 - p_{\text{lower}} = 1 - 0.8609 = 0.1391 \implies 13.91\%\]
  \[\text{Mean Failure Interval} = \frac{1}{0.1391} \approx 7.19 \text{ trials}\]
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Conclusion:} The observation ``20 out of 20 passed'' permits the
machine to fail once every \(7.2\) runs under sustained operation.

\end{fbxSimple}

This gap separates an empirical record from a statistical population
claim. The statement that twenty out of twenty trials passed is an
immutable historical observation. It describes what occurred on a
particular physical chassis on a specific surface, under a fixed set of
lighting conditions, with a freshly charged battery pack, on a single
afternoon. The statement that the policy succeeds with probability at
least \(p\) is a forward-looking claim about future performance over an
operational design domain. Translating the historical record into a
forward-looking guarantee requires assuming that the test environment
matches the operational domain, that physical dynamics do not drift, and
that twenty trials provide enough statistical mass to characterize rare
failure modes.

An evaluation measurement never characterizes a learned policy in
isolation. Every claim about policy performance depends jointly on five
concrete elements: the specific compiled model weights (\(\pi_\theta\)),
the individual physical machine and its mechanical wear (\(m\)), the
distribution of environmental conditions (\(e\)), the formal outcome
rule that defines what constitutes success (\(\phi\)), and the exact
sampling protocol used to initialize each run
(\(s_0 \sim \mathcal{D}\)). Altering the ambient room temperature,
substituting a tire with slightly lower friction, or shifting the
initial yaw angle by two degrees changes the distribution of state
transitions. Without explicitly conditioning on all five elements, an
observed success rate is an unmoored number.

This principle holds across all three canonical Physical AI archetypes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Mobile systems (e.g., wheeled rovers, quadrotors, autonomous
  vehicles).} A twenty-run obstacle avoidance test on dry concrete at
  \(20^\circ\text{C}\) provides zero statistical license for operations
  on wet epoxy flooring (\(\Delta \mu = -0.55\)) or under direct solar
  glare (\(10^5\text{ lx}\)) that saturates optical cameras.
\item
  \emph{Manipulators (e.g., 6-DoF/7-DoF robotic arms, insertion
  mechanisms).} Twenty flawless peg-in-hole insertions on clean steel
  components reveal nothing about performance when thermal expansion
  shifts link lengths by \(0.15\text{ mm}\) or when surface burrs
  increase insertion friction.
\item
  \emph{Process \& energy systems (e.g., thermal management loops,
  chemical reactors, power grid inverters).} Twenty successful
  temperature regulation cycles under nominal electrical loads provide
  no guarantee against thermal runaway when ambient cooling capacity
  degrades by \(20\%\) during peak summer ambient temperatures.
\end{itemize}

Pre-deployment evaluation encounters three structural limits when
applied to machines that interact with the physical world. First, static
or open-loop evaluations on recorded datasets fail to reflect feedback.
A policy executing in the physical loop alters its own state trajectory,
where minor tracking errors accumulate over time and push the machine
into unmodeled regions of state space where the learned policy behaves
unpredictably. Second, finite physical testing budgets leave wide
statistical bounds. Demonstrating that a machine satisfies a high
reliability target, such as a failure rate below one in ten thousand
runs (\(P_{99.99}\)), requires tens of thousands of physical trials that
are impractical to execute before release. Third, deployment changes the
encountered distribution. Because a learned policy actively chooses
which states the machine visits, the policy itself shapes the
operational distribution it encounters, creating closed-loop
distribution shift.

The \textbf{predeployment evaluation boundary} is the formal statistical
and physical limitation governing empirical verification, establishing
that an observed sample success rate \(\hat{p}\) on finite trials
(\(n\)) supports only a conditional claim over explicitly sampled
environmental distributions (\(c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa)\))
and non-asymptotic confidence bounds
(\(p_{\text{lower}} = \alpha^{1/n}\)), leaving unvisited dynamical
states and endogenous closed-loop feedback uncertified prior to
deployment.

These constraints do not diminish the necessity of pre-deployment
evaluation, but they bound what it can establish. Evaluation before
deployment provides valuable negative evidence and supports well-defined
conditional claims. It systematically surfaces kinematic limits,
identifies perception failures caused by sensor noise, reveals numerical
instabilities in the inference pipeline, and validates behavior within
the specific envelopes covered by the test protocol. Evaluation
demonstrates that the policy operates correctly across tested instances,
but it cannot prove that the policy will remain safe across unvisited
states.

Because testing before deployment cannot verify safety across the
unbounded variety of the physical world, the limits of evaluation define
an architectural requirement for the machine. What cannot be proved
before deployment must be observed and constrained during operation. The
nervous system cannot treat the learned policy as a guaranteed
controller based on an empirical pass rate. Instead, it must
continuously monitor physical states, observe system invariants, and
enforce safety boundaries in real time, retaining the authority to
reject actions whenever the machine approaches the limits of its
physical operating envelope.

\section{What You Are Actually Measuring}\label{sec-evaluation-7-2}

An evaluation benchmark routinely reports a single summary statistic,
such as an eighty-five percent success rate on an obstacle avoidance
task. In machine learning practice, that number is often treated as an
intrinsic score belonging to the learned model weights, analogous to
top-one accuracy on a static image classification dataset. In a physical
machine, that interpretation is invalid. A learned policy has no
independent physical performance. What the benchmark measured was the
closed-loop execution of an entire physical system across a specific
sequence of days and environmental states. Success rate is an empirical
property of the coupled system, comprising the policy, the mechanical
plant, the onboard computational hardware, the operating environment,
and the trial protocol.

To evaluate a policy, an engineering team executes a sequence of
discrete physical runs. A single trial is fully determined only when
every variable that can alter the physical state trajectory is fixed or
explicitly sampled. Formally, let a single trial condition be defined by
a tuple \(c = (s_0, e, m, \pi_\theta, \kappa)\), drawn from an
operational testing distribution \(\mathcal{D}\). The vector \(s_0\)
represents the initial state of the machine, including position, linear
velocity, angular orientation, and actuator positions. The environment
vector \(e\) captures external variables such as floor friction, ambient
illuminance, obstacle geometry, and ambient air temperature. The machine
state \(m\) captures physical and hardware properties, including battery
state of charge, payload mass, tire wear, mechanical backlash in the
drivetrain, and sensor calibration parameters. The computational
configuration \(\pi_\theta\) encompasses the frozen policy weights
\(\theta\), inference quantization, scheduling deadlines, and software
versions. Finally, the termination protocol
\(\kappa = (T_{\max}, g, \phi)\) defines the execution time limit
\(T_{\max}\), the spatial goal region \(g\), and the binary evaluation
function \(\phi\) that maps the resulting trajectory to a terminal
outcome \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\).

The true success probability of the system under this evaluation
protocol is the expectation of the binary outcome over the joint
distribution of trial conditions:
\[p(\mathcal{D}) = \mathbb{E}_{c \sim \mathcal{D}}\left[ \phi(\text{Traj}(c)) \right] = \int \phi(\text{Traj}(c)) \, p(c) \, dc\]
In this formulation, \(\text{Traj}(c)\) is the continuous physical
trajectory produced when the policy \(\pi_\theta\) executes within the
physical environment and hardware state defined by \(c\). This
expectation demonstrates why \(p(\mathcal{D})\) cannot be treated as a
measurement of \(\theta\) alone. The model weights \(\theta\) constitute
only one parameter inside the condition vector \(c\). If the
distribution over floor friction \(p(e)\) shifts, or if the distribution
over initial battery charge \(p(m)\) changes, the value of the integral
\(p(\mathcal{D})\) changes while \(\theta\) remains identical. The
sampling protocol is not an external apparatus measuring an isolated
model; it is part of the mathematical quantity being estimated.

The physical mechanisms that alter \(c\) between trials operate
independently of the policy:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  In \emph{Mobile systems.}, a lithium-ion battery pack at ninety
  percent state of charge provides higher terminal voltage to the motor
  drivers than a depleted pack at twenty percent state of charge. As
  terminal voltage drops under high load, the maximum achievable motor
  torque decreases according to the electromechanical torque-speed
  curve. If a trajectory demands a peak acceleration of
  \(1.2\text{ m/s}^2\) to clear a moving obstacle, the robot clears the
  obstacle when the battery is fully charged, but understeers and
  collides when the battery is depleted. Similarly, ambient sunlight
  shifting across an afternoon changes camera exposure times from
  \(2\text{ ms}\) to \(20\text{ ms}\). This tenfold increase introduces
  motion blur during turning maneuvers, corrupting feature extraction in
  the visual backbone and causing state estimation drift. Floor dust
  accumulation lowers the static friction coefficient from
  \(\mu = 0.80\) to \(\mu = 0.55\), extending the stopping distance from
  an initial speed of \(2.0\text{ m/s}\) from \(0.26\text{ m}\) to
  \(0.37\text{ m}\).
\item
  In \emph{Manipulator systems.}, continuous high-speed pick-and-place
  cycles generate Joule heating in harmonic drive gearboxes, heating
  lubricant and altering friction damping coefficients by over \(25\%\).
  As structural linkages warm, thermal expansion shifts
  tool-center-point (TCP) kinematic calibration by
  \(0.15\text{–}0.30\text{ mm}\). A policy trained to insert a peg into
  a chamfered hole with \(0.20\text{ mm}\) clearance succeeds during
  early morning cold starts but jams repeatedly in the afternoon as
  thermal growth exhausts kinematic tolerance margins.
\item
  In \emph{Process \& energy systems.}, ambient temperature swings alter
  the thermal gradient across cooling heat exchangers. A neural policy
  regulating chiller pump speeds that maintains coolant temperature
  below \(45^\circ\text{C}\) in a \(20^\circ\text{C}\) laboratory
  environment fails when ambient air hits \(38^\circ\text{C}\),
  triggering high-pressure compressor trips despite executing identical
  control laws.
\end{itemize}

In all these cases, the policy weights and input tensor shapes are
identical, yet the physical trajectory transitions from success to
failure.

Non-model variation also enters through the reset procedure and operator
handling. When human operators manually reposition a machine between
trials, they introduce subtle spatial biases. If an operator
instinctively resets the robot facing open space after a difficult run,
the empirical distribution of initial heading angles shifts toward
favorable states. Conversely, an automated reset procedure that
repeatedly drives the machine along a fixed path induces cyclic heating
in the actuator windings, increasing electrical resistance and reducing
actuator response speed across successive trials. If an operator
intervenes to catch a falling machine and discards the run as an
unrecorded reset, the hardest failure modes are erased from the sample
history, artificially inflating the observed success rate.

Statistical evaluation requires distinguishing ordinary sampling
variation from a change in the underlying estimand. When \(N\) trials
are drawn from a fixed distribution \(\mathcal{D}\), the sample
proportion \(\hat{p} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i\) fluctuates around
the true parameter \(p(\mathcal{D})\) due to random sampling noise. This
uncertainty can be bounded using standard statistical estimators.
However, if an evaluation changes the payload mass from
\(0.0\text{ kg}\) to \(5.0\text{ kg}\), or shifts testing from dry
concrete to wet asphalt, the experiment is no longer drawing samples
from \(\mathcal{D}\). It is sampling from an entirely different
distribution \(\mathcal{D}'\), defined by a new parameter
\(p(\mathcal{D}')\). Treating data collected under \(\mathcal{D}'\) as
an extension of the original sample pool conflates sampling variance
with structural bias, combining observations from two different physical
machines.

Because success probability is defined only with respect to a specific
joint distribution \(\mathcal{D}\), the intended operating envelope must
be declared before trials are sampled. In systems engineering, this
envelope is the \textbf{operational design domain} (ODD). If an
engineering team executes fifty physical runs across ad hoc trajectories
and reports a ninety percent pass rate, the denominator corresponds to
an undefined population. A measured success rate is statistically
meaningful only when the support and density of \(\mathcal{D}\) are
specified in advance, establishing explicit bounds on illuminance,
payload ranges, surface friction coefficients, and allowable initial
state offsets. Without an explicit prior specification of
\(\mathcal{D}\), an evaluation can be made arbitrarily successful by
restricting test runs to benign regions of the operating envelope.

Extracting valid confidence bounds from empirical trials requires three
operational conditions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Independent and Identically Distributed Sampling:} Trials must
  be independent realizations drawn from \(\mathcal{D}\). If thermal
  accumulation in motor windings or progressive mechanical wear degrades
  hardware efficiency across consecutive runs, trial outcomes become
  negatively correlated over time, violating independence.
\item
  \emph{Fixed Outcome Predicates:} The binary evaluation function
  \(\phi\) and the termination criteria \(\kappa\) must remain fixed
  throughout the campaign. Modifying the time horizon \(T_{\max}\) or
  adjusting the spatial tolerance of the goal region \(g\) midway
  through testing alters the definition of success.
\item
  \emph{Full-Denominator Accounting:} Every initiated run that aborts
  due to hardware faults, communication timeouts, or emergency stops
  must be recorded as a failure (\(Y = 0\)). Dropping aborted trials
  substitutes a measure of conditional execution on surviving hardware
  for the true operational reliability of the machine.
\end{enumerate}

When these conditions are strictly enforced, physical trials yield an
unbiased sample mean for the closed-loop system under the tested
distribution \(\mathcal{D}\). Yet physical testing remains constrained
by hardware wear, operator labor, and wall-clock execution time. To
bypass these constraints, evaluation workflows often turn to open-loop
evaluations on recorded datasets, calculating how accurately a candidate
policy reproduces logged expert actions offline. That substitution
assumes that a model that predicts demonstrated actions with high
statistical accuracy will exhibit equivalent competence when granted
real-time authority over a physical machine.

\section{Open Loop and Closed Loop}\label{sec-evaluation-7-3}

In an \textbf{open-loop evaluation}, a candidate policy \(\pi_\theta\)
is scored across a static dataset of recorded demonstrations
\(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}} = \{(s_t^*, a_t^*)\}_{t=1}^T\). At each
discrete timestep \(t\), the policy receives a recorded demonstrator
state \(s_t^*\) and outputs a predicted action
\(\hat{a}_t = \pi_\theta(s_t^*)\). An error metric, such as mean squared
error or cross-entropy, measures the distance between \(\hat{a}_t\) and
the recorded expert action \(a_t^*\). At step \(t+1\), the evaluation
pipeline supplies the next recorded state \(s_{t+1}^*\) from the
dataset. The action \(\hat{a}_t\) produced by the policy is discarded
without executing on hardware, keeping the sequence of input states
independent of the policy's past outputs. In a \textbf{closed-loop
evaluation}, the policy is coupled directly to the state-transition
recurrence \(s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t)\). The action
\(a_t = \pi_\theta(s_t)\) commanded by the policy executes on the
physical plant, altering the state trajectory and making the policy
responsible for the observations it receives at subsequent timesteps.

Because open-loop evaluation tests actions only along the demonstrator's
state trajectory, a policy that scores low prediction error offline can
fail immediately when granted authority over physical motion
(\citeproc{ref-ross2011reduction}{Ross et al. 2011};
\citeproc{ref-pomerleau1989alvinn}{Pomerleau 1989}). Consider an
analytical example of a planar moving platform tracking a straight
corridor of length \(L = 10\text{ m}\) at a constant forward speed of
\(v = 1.0\text{ m/s}\). The nominal expert demonstration follows the
centerline with heading \(\theta^* = 0\text{ rad}\) and lateral offset
\(y^* = 0\text{ m}\) for a duration of \(10\text{ s}\). The policy runs
at a control frequency of \(10\text{ Hz}\), executing updates every
\(\Delta t = 0.1\text{ s}\) across \(100\) discrete steps. Suppose the
candidate policy has a systematic heading bias of
\(\epsilon_\theta = 1.0^\circ\) (\(0.01745\text{ rad}\)) on every step.

In an open-loop evaluation, the policy receives the demonstrator state
\(s_t^* = (x_t^*, 0, 0)\) at each step and predicts a forward velocity
with a \(1.0^\circ\) steering offset. The offline scoring pipeline
records a mean absolute angular error of \(1.0^\circ\), or a mean
squared error of
\(\text{MSE} = (0.01745)^2 \approx 3.05 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad}^2\).
By standard regression metrics, this policy appears to match the expert
with \(99.7\%\) directional accuracy. In closed-loop execution, however,
the state evolves under the kinematic relation
\(\dot{y} = v \sin(\theta)\). A constant heading deviation of
\(1.0^\circ\) produces a lateral velocity of:
\[v_y = 1.0\text{ m/s} \times \sin(1.0^\circ) \approx 0.01745\text{ m/s}\]
Over the \(10\text{ m}\) transit (\(10\text{ s}\) duration), this
velocity produces a cumulative lateral displacement:
\[y(10\text{ s}) = \int_0^{10} v \sin(\epsilon_\theta) \, dt = 10\text{ s} \times 0.01745\text{ m/s} \approx 0.1745\text{ m} = 17.5\text{ cm}\]
If the corridor provides \(15.0\text{ cm}\) of clearance to a side
boundary, the platform collides with the wall at \(t = 8.6\text{ s}\)
after traveling \(8.6\text{ m}\)
(\(y(8.6\text{ s}) = 8.6 \times 0.01745 = 0.150\text{ m}\)). The policy
achieves an open-loop error of \(0.0175\text{ rad}\) and a closed-loop
task success rate of zero percent.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-ruleux2a-7.5}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-rule}{Architect’s Rule of Thumb:}{Open-Loop Blindness}
\phantomsection\label{callout-rule*-7.5}

Open-loop loss measures dataset mimicry; closed-loop dynamics decide
physical survival. A policy with near-zero offline prediction error will
diverge catastrophically the instant an uncorrected action bias
integrates through the physical plant.

\end{fbxSimple}

The \textbf{offline-online evaluation disconnect} is the fundamental
decoupling of open-loop dataset loss metrics (such as action mean
squared error or imitation log-likelihood on static logs) from
closed-loop physical stability and task survival, caused by the
inability of static evaluation to reflect compounding kinematic
integration errors
(\(y(t) \approx \int_0^t v \sin \epsilon_\theta \, d\tau\)) and
self-induced distribution shift during embodied execution.

This divergence occurs because open-loop evaluation resets the machine
to an expert state at every clock cycle, masking the compounding nature
of integration errors. In closed loop, the state at index \(t\) is the
expanded composition of all previous actions:
\[s_t = f(f(\dots f(s_0, a_0)\dots, a_{t-2}), a_{t-1})\] The first minor
action error shifts the physical machine from the demonstrated state
\(s_1^*\) to an unvisited state \(s_1\). Once the platform drifts
\(2.0\text{ cm}\) off nominal, it enters a state that does not appear
anywhere in \(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{demo}}\). Because the policy was
evaluated only on demonstrator states where \(y = 0\text{ m}\), the
offline metric contains no evidence regarding what action
\(\pi_\theta(s)\) the policy will produce when \(y \neq 0\text{ m}\). If
the training distribution lacked demonstrations of recovery maneuvers
from off-center coordinates, the policy can output larger corrective
errors, accelerating the divergence instead of arresting it.

This disconnect manifests across all physical machine archetypes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Mobile Systems:} As derived above, a \(1.0^\circ\) angular error
  integrates across \(10\text{ m}\) into a \(17.5\text{ cm}\) lateral
  offset, breaching corridor clearance limits.
\item
  \emph{Manipulator Systems:} An end-effector position error of
  \(0.5\text{ mm}\) per step during a contact assembly task (e.g.,
  chamfered pin insertion) appears negligible on offline Cartesian MSE.
  In closed-loop contact, that \(0.5\text{ mm}\) displacement drives the
  pin against the chamfer rim, generating high lateral reaction forces
  that jam the joint and trip the robot's torque limits
  (\(F_z > F_{\max}\)).
\item
  \emph{Process \& Energy Systems:} A temperature prediction error of
  \(0.5^\circ\text{C}\) per minute in an industrial reactor cooling
  policy seems minor on offline logs. In closed loop, failing to
  increase coolant flow compounds thermal accumulation, driving reactor
  core temperature past the safe \(95^\circ\text{C}\) trip threshold
  within twenty minutes.
\end{itemize}

The relationship between offline and online metrics is directional.
Open-loop evaluation is optimistically blind to compounding trajectory
divergence and unvisited state instabilities, because it assumes an
external mechanism continuously restores the machine to the expert path.
Conversely, open-loop action metrics can be pessimistic when the
physical task permits multiple valid actions. If a human demonstrator
avoided an obstacle by steering left, an open-loop evaluation penalizes
a candidate policy that steers right, recording a large action error
against \(a_t^*\). In closed-loop execution, passing on the right clears
the obstacle and reaches the target state with equal validity. An
action-level prediction error measures divergence from a specific
demonstration recording, not the satisfaction of the physical task.

As illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig-07-open-vs-closed-loop}, open-loop
evaluation evaluates candidate actions only on demonstrator states where
errors are immediately discarded, obscuring the cumulative trajectory
divergence that drives closed-loop physical execution into catastrophic
wall collisions.

(b) In closed-loop physical execution, the unmodeled angular bias
