command register• \textbf{Plant:} Real-time host model & Instruction
cache evictions, register corruption via JTAG/BIST, interrupt jitter
injection & \(0.1\text{--}1.0\times\) real-time; bound by cross-platform
synchronization & Instruction-set and compiler accurate; abstracts
analog bus lines and actuator back-EMF & \textbf{Oracle:} Target
register state and WCET execution bounds.\textbf{Limit:} Ignores
physical transceiver bus contention, voltage droop, and thermal rise. \\
\textbf{Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL)}\emph{(Target ECUs + Real-Time Plant
Rig)} & • \textbf{Compute:} Production ECU / NPU• \textbf{Bus:} Real
physical CAN/Ethernet• \textbf{Actuator:} Real motor drives / dyno•
\textbf{Plant:} Hard real-time FPGA plant rig & Pin break/short, CAN
frame stuffing / babbling idiot, supply rail droop, load steps &
\(1.0\times\) strict real-time (\(24\text{ h/day}\) wall-clock limit) &
High electrical, timing, and protocol fidelity; bounded by FPGA plant
model accuracy & \textbf{Oracle:} Protocol CRC, bus deadline monitors,
and interlock timings.\textbf{Limit:} Cannot execute destructive
physical overload or simulate micro-cavitation wear. \\
\textbf{Physical Fault Rig \& Shadow}\emph{(Dynamometer Cell / Field
Plant)} & • \textbf{Compute:} Production ECU / NPU• \textbf{Bus:}
Production harness \& sensors• \textbf{Actuator:} Real physical
mechanisms• \textbf{Plant:} Real fluid / mechanical body & Pyrotechnic
valve jammers, magnetic brake stall, thermal heating, transducer bias
drift & \(1.0\times\) wall-clock; constrained by mechanical wear and
thermal reset (\(<10^3\text{ cycles/day}\)) & Full authentic physics
(Coulomb friction, acoustic wave shock, thermal dissipation, wear) &
\textbf{Oracle:} Independent physical containment instrumentation and
yield transducers.\textbf{Limit:} High financial cost per trial;
destructive tests cannot scale to statistical tail bounds. \\
\end{longtable}

To prevent false confidence, every reported verification result must
explicitly state which elements of the causal loop were physically real,
which were simulated, which were replayed from static logs, which were
bypassed, and which remained unobserved. An analytical engineering claim
that an intervention mechanism halted an overpressure event within
\(12\text{ ms}\) means nothing without specifying whether the pressure
signal was generated by a differential equation, transmitted over a
physical analog current loop, or replayed from a digital buffer.
Specifying this causal mapping exposes the assumptions underlying each
test, ensuring that unmodeled physics or artificial boundary conditions
do not disguise latent hazards.

The \textbf{causal-loop fidelity boundary} defines the structural
demarcation between the physical mechanisms and digital abstractions
exercised within a given test environment, defining the exact threshold
where synthetic models, emulated buses, or replayed sensor traces sever
the continuous bi-directional energy and information exchange between
compute and mechanics.

Once the test environment is defined and its causal boundaries are
accounted for, the qualification process requires concrete mechanisms to
evaluate whether the machine behavior during a fault injection
constitutes a pass or a failure.

\section{Fault Oracles and Acceptance
Criteria}\label{sec-verification-15-5}

A fault test without a precommitted detector and an acceptable response
is an anecdote about a machine that did something. When a fault is
injected into a running machine, the system will inevitably react,
producing telemetry transients, actuator motions, and acoustic
emissions. Without an unambiguous, pre-established oracle to evaluate
those reactions, engineers evaluate the result by looking at time-series
plots after the run, deciding whether the machine survived based on
whether any component burst or threw an unhandled exception. An
\textbf{oracle} is the mathematical predicate that evaluates a test
execution and returns a binary verdict of pass or fail, defined in full
before the execution begins.

In physical AI systems, evaluating whether a machine satisfied its
safety claims requires moving beyond static scalar bounds to continuous
temporal specifications. Physical systems do not fail at single isolated
instants; they fail through dynamic transients over time. To express and
verify these dynamic properties rigorously, verification engineering
uses \textbf{Signal Temporal Logic (STL)}. Given a continuous-time
cyber-physical trajectory \(\mathbf{x}: [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^n\)
capturing state variables (e.g., fluid pressure \(P(t)\), flow rate
\(Q(t)\), actuator temperature \(T_{\text{coil}}(t)\)), an STL formula
\(\phi\) is constructed from atomic predicates
\(\mu \equiv (g(\mathbf{x}(t)) \ge 0)\), standard Boolean connectives,
and metric real-time temporal operators:
\[\phi := \mu \mid \neg \phi \mid \phi_1 \wedge \phi_2 \mid \phi_1 \vee \phi_2 \mid \square_{[a, b]} \phi \mid \Diamond_{[a, b]} \phi \mid \phi_1 \mathcal{U}_{[a, b]} \phi_2\]
where \(\square_{[a, b]}\) denotes the \emph{Always} operator (the
formula must hold at every time \(t' \in [t+a, t+b]\)),
\(\Diamond_{[a, b]}\) denotes the \emph{Eventually} operator (the
formula must hold at some time \(t' \in [t+a, t+b]\)), and
\(\mathcal{U}_{[a, b]}\) denotes the timed \emph{Until} operator.

Crucially, STL equips verification with \textbf{quantitative robustness
semantics}, defining a real-valued metric
\(\rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, t) \in \mathbb{R}\) that measures not merely
\emph{whether} the specification held, but \emph{how far} the trajectory
remained from violating it: \[\begin{aligned}
\rho(\mu, \mathbf{x}, t) &= g(\mathbf{x}(t)) \\
\rho(\neg \phi, \mathbf{x}, t) &= -\rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, t) \\
\rho(\phi_1 \wedge \phi_2, \mathbf{x}, t) &= \min\left(\rho(\phi_1, \mathbf{x}, t), \rho(\phi_2, \mathbf{x}, t)\right) \\
\rho(\phi_1 \vee \phi_2, \mathbf{x}, t) &= \max\left(\rho(\phi_1, \mathbf{x}, t), \rho(\phi_2, \mathbf{x}, t)\right) \\
\rho(\square_{[a, b]} \phi, \mathbf{x}, t) &= \min_{t' \in [t+a, t+b]} \rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, t') \\
\rho(\Diamond_{[a, b]} \phi, \mathbf{x}, t) &= \max_{t' \in [t+a, t+b]} \rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, t')
\end{aligned}\]

The quantitative robustness metric satisfies the foundational soundness
property: \[\begin{cases}
\rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, 0) > 0 \implies \mathbf{x} \models \phi & (\text{Specification satisfied with physical margin } \rho) \\
\rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, 0) < 0 \implies \mathbf{x} \not\models \phi & (\text{Specification violated by physical depth } |\rho|) \\
\rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, 0) = 0 & (\text{Trajectory on critical failure boundary})
\end{cases}\]

Consider a high-pressure manifold regulating coolant flow at
\(10.0\text{ bar}\) with a nominal throughput of \(5.0\text{ L/s}\).
When a downstream valve jams under a \(15.0\text{ bar}\) head, the
physical safety requirement is formalized in STL as:
\[\phi_{\text{safe}} = \square_{[0, T]} \left( P(t) \le 16.5\text{ bar} \right) \wedge \square_{[0, T - 200\text{ ms}]} \left( \Diamond_{[0, 45\text{ ms}]} \left( Q_{\text{bypass}}(t) \ge 3.5\text{ L/s} \right) \right)\]
This formula states that at all times during the trial, line pressure
must remain below the \(16.5\text{ bar}\) containment limit, and
whenever a disturbance occurs, the bypass flow must exceed
\(3.5\text{ L/s}\) within \(45\text{ ms}\). If an injected fault causes
the peak pressure to reach \(17.2\text{ bar}\), the quantitative
robustness evaluates to
\(\rho(\phi_{\text{safe}}, \mathbf{x}, 0) = 16.5 - 17.2 = -0.7\text{ bar}\),
immediately quantifying the failure severity without manual inspection.

Quantitative semantics transforms whole-system verification from
unguided random testing into \textbf{temporal logic falsification as
adversarial optimization}. Because neural network policies operate
across high-dimensional continuous state spaces, uniform random sampling
(Monte Carlo fuzzing) requires an intractable number of trials to
encounter rare failure modes. By formulating the verification goal as
minimizing the STL robustness metric over a parameterized disturbance
space \(\mathcal{W}\), an automated falsification engine actively
searches for the worst-case disturbance vector \(\mathbf{w}^*\):
\[\mathbf{w}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{W}} \rho\left(\phi, \mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{w}}, 0\right)\]
where \(\mathbf{w}\) parameterizes disturbance parameters such as sensor
noise variance, network packet arrival jitter, supply voltage droop
depth, initial fluid temperature, and valve spool friction coefficients.

Falsification engines employ global black-box optimization
algorithms---including Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy
(CMA-ES), Bayesian Optimization with Gaussian Process surrogates, and
the Cross-Entropy Method---to navigate non-convex, discontinuous
cyber-physical landscapes. In differentiable simulation environments,
analytical gradients \(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \rho\) can be computed via
automatic differentiation through the neural policy and differentiable
physics simulator, enabling gradient-directed falsification. When the
optimization algorithm finds
\(\rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{w}^*}, 0) < 0\), it produces a
concrete, deterministic counterexample trajectory that falsifies the
safety claim, exposing the exact combination of physical disturbance and
latency that breaks the machine.

Alongside the pass and fail criteria, automated verification requires an
\textbf{invalid-test rule} that identifies when an experimental run must
be discarded rather than scored. A test run is invalid whenever the
execution environment fails to deliver the specified fault conditions or
violates the required operational preconditions. If an upstream supply
pump cavitates before the planned fault injection timestamp, lowering
the baseline manifold pressure to \(6.0\text{ bar}\) instead of the
required \(10.0\text{ bar} \pm 0.2\text{ bar}\), the test did not
evaluate the safety envelope under high-head conditions. Similarly, if
an injection framework injecting corrupted CAN frames suffers an
internal queue overflow and drops the fault packet before it reaches the
transceiver, the system under test was never subjected to the
disturbance. Scoring an unexercised run as a pass manufactures false
confidence, while scoring it as a failure penalizes the machine for an
error in the test fixture. The invalid-test rule codifies the boundary
conditions, rejecting the run and resetting the test sequence whenever
preconditions fail.

Precommitment is the engineering discipline that separates verifiable
evidence from post-hoc storytelling. When an assembled machine undergoes
physical or electrical fault injection, the resulting behavior is almost
always noisy, complex, and surprising. If acceptance criteria are
negotiated after observing the machine react, human engineers
systematically rationalize anomalies. An unexpected pressure oscillation
of \(17.5\text{ bar}\) is explained away as an acceptable structural
surge, or a \(60\text{ ms}\) reaction delay is excused because the
system eventually brought the flow back to steady state without tripping
the mechanical burst disc. Post-hoc evaluation converts safety
verification into a negotiation, where the definition of success drifts
to match whatever the machine happened to do.

Precommitment demands that the STL specification \(\phi\), the
robustness evaluation function \(\rho\), the response-time bounds, and
the invalidation triggers are compiled into immutable test code before
the first injection run is scheduled. When the test executes, the
automated evaluation framework samples the instrumentation, computes
\(\rho(\phi, \mathbf{x}, 0)\), and outputs a deterministic verdict
without human intervention. If the machine breaches the precommitted
state boundary by \(0.1\text{ bar}\) or exceeds the response deadline by
\(2\text{ ms}\), the run is recorded as a failure, pointing directly to
an inadequate control margin or a slow diagnostic filter in the nervous
system.

Establishing precommitted oracles and quantitative temporal logic
boundaries transforms fault injection from a qualitative demonstration
into a quantitative measurement of system margins. Yet the validity of
that measurement remains entirely dependent on whether the injected
disturbances and the monitored reactions interact through real physical
dynamics or through mathematical approximations. Defining the exact
boundaries of a valid test and the criteria for success prepares the
engineering team to confront the physical machine itself, where
synthetic models give way to the unyielding mechanics of real hardware.

\section{Fault Injection on Hardware}\label{sec-verification-15-6}

A fault injected in simulation tests the simulator. When a disturbance
is synthesized inside a mathematical model, the software reacts against
the numerical assumptions that the modeler wrote down. Digital
simulations assume ideal clock synchronization, perfectly isolated
memory addresses, deterministic context switches, and linear
communication delays across shared interconnects. In the physical
machine, faults do not execute inside isolated functions. They propagate
across physical silicon, where memory access contention on a shared
system bus, clock drift between asynchronous microcontrollers, direct
memory access stalls, and voltage drops across inductive actuator
drivers dictate whether an intervention executes in time. To establish
evidence that survives scrutiny, fault injection must be performed
directly on target hardware through the production handoff, driving
disturbances through physical transceivers, target timers, shared buses,
and the hardware enforcement path, while an independent containment rig
protects the test facility from physical destruction.

\textbf{In-situ fault injection} is the deliberate, deterministic
introduction of physical, electrical, and computational disturbances
(including sensor register latches, clock drift, bus contention, supply
brownouts, and actuator load stalls) directly into target production
silicon and mechanics while operating under authentic electrical,
thermal, and dynamic loads.

Full-scale hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test facilities
(Figure~\ref{fig-15-hil-avionics-testbed}) bridge this reality gap by
mounting production Electronic Control Units (ECUs) and actuator drivers
in their authentic physical flight geometry, connecting real
line-replaceable units through physical wiring harnesses, power
distribution channels, and breakout interfaces to real-time
fault-injection racks.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-decisionux2a-15.4}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-decision}{Design Decision:}{Testbed Instrumentation Architecture}
\phantomsection\label{callout-decision*-15.4}

Physical testbed verification requires dedicated bench instrumentation
engineered to intercept, corrupt, and observe signals without altering
circuit impedance or timing characteristics. A fully instrumented
physical AI verification testbed integrates five specialized hardware
subsystems:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{High-Bandwidth Digital Storage Oscilloscopes (DSOs) and Logic
  Analyzers:} Synchronized across common \(10\text{ MHz}\) reference
  clocks to capture microsecond-level transitions across SPI, CAN, and
  gate-driver PWM lines.
\item
  \textbf{Inline Breakout Injection Boxes:} Equipped with solid-state
  Field-Effect Transistor (FET) switches capable of sub-microsecond
  pin-level open-circuit disconnections, short-to-ground, and
  short-to-power faults.
\item
  \textbf{Programmable Fieldbus Disturbance Nodes:} Dedicated
  microcontrollers capable of injecting bit-level CAN frame stuffing,
  cyclic redundancy check (CRC) corruptions, and unthrottled
  ``babbling-idiot'' message floods.
\item
  \textbf{Precision Programmable DC Power Supplies and Electronic
  Loads:} Capable of synthesizing fast supply rail droops
  (\(V_{\text{core}} < 0.85\text{ V}\)), ground bounce, and inrush
  current transients under dynamic motor loading.
\item
  \textbf{External Truth Transducers:} Laser Doppler vibrometers,
  optical shaft encoders, and high-speed photogrammetric cameras wired
  to isolated digitizers, recording ground-truth physical motion
  independent of the embedded controllers under test.
\end{enumerate}

\end{fbxSimple}

Consider a high-pressure fluid loop where an electric control valve
regulates a mass flow rate of \(12.0\text{ kg/s}\) across a differential
pressure of \(30.0\text{ bar}\). In this analytical example, the
downstream accumulator has a volume of \(0.04\text{ m}^3\) and an
effective fluid bulk modulus of \(1.6\times 10^9\text{ Pa}\). If the
valve stem shifts unexpectedly by \(2.0\text{ mm}\), the resulting mass
flow imbalance causes downstream pressure to rise at an analytical rate
of \(80.0\text{ bar/s}\), which consumes the entire \(0.8\text{ bar}\)
allowable transient margin in exactly \(10\text{ ms}\). In a digital
simulator, verifying that the nervous system catches this excursion
requires only checking an assertion statement. On production silicon,
verifying the response requires injecting the disturbance into the
physical sensor interface. When the test fixture injects a stale
observation by holding the analog-to-digital converter (ADC) output
constant while maintaining the original acquisition timestamp, the test
evaluates whether the freshness detector on the real-time safety
microcontroller (MCU) identifies the stall within its budgeted
\(P_{99}\) latency of \(4.0\text{ ms}\). If the detector relies on a
software timer that shares an interrupt line with a busy network
interface, the arrival of background telemetry can delay the interrupt
handler by \(8\text{ ms}\), allowing the stale state estimate to persist
until the pressure breaches the physical containment boundary.

Testing the heterogeneous Dual-Brain architecture---where an
unprivileged Linux host (MPU) generates learned neural proposals while a
deterministic real-time microcontroller (MCU) enforces safety
bounds---demands physical fault injection directly at their
inter-processor boundary:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Stale Observation Injection:} An inline FPGA interceptor
  latches an ADC register or suppresses CAN frame updates while
  preserving the original hardware timestamp. This evaluates whether the
  MCU's temporal freshness monitor detects the frozen observation within
  its \(\Delta t_{\text{det}} \le 4.0\text{ ms}\) budget before stale
  state estimates degrade actuator commands.
\item
  \textbf{Late Plan Injection:} The injection testbed delays neural
  trajectory proposals across the MPU-to-MCU shared memory bridge. If a
  proposal scheduled for execution at \(t = 100\text{ ms}\) arrives at
  \(t = 106\text{ ms}\), the test verifies that the MCU's deterministic
  scheduler instantly refuses the late submission, clamps the actuator
  to a precommitted safe hold position, and transitions the loop to
  deterministic fallback before physical vessel margins expire.
\item
  \textbf{Expired Intent Lease Revocation:} The test framework
  deliberately suppresses the cryptographic lease renewal packet
  transmitted by the Linux MPU. The verification oracle confirms that
  the MCU hardware gate revokes proposal authority on the exact clock
  cycle of lease expiry (\(t = 20.0\text{ ms}\) in
  Figure~\ref{fig-15-hardware-fault-injection}), immediately dropping
  un-leased commands even if their setpoints appear numerically
  plausible and smooth.
\end{itemize}

Recording the resulting state trajectory, the detector identity, the
exact refusal timestamp, and the time required to restore the bounded
state requires instrumentation that is electrically and logically
independent of the machine under test. If the test engineer relies on
the onboard logging daemon to measure reaction times, the measurement is
corrupted by the very failure it attempts to capture, because a faulted
CPU or a saturated bus delays log serialization.\sidenote{\footnotesize On safety
  microcontrollers (ARM Cortex-R5F, Infineon AURIX), dedicated fault
  injection registers and BIST controllers flip SRAM bits to verify that
  ECC SECDED triggers an immediate Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) before
  corrupted coordinates reach actuator PWM registers.} Furthermore,
independent measurement prevents the acceptance of false passes where
the machine survived for reasons absent from the safety claim. A
documented example occurred during ground qualification testing of the
Apollo guidance computer, where simulated testing failed to uncover an
asynchronous memory-bus stealing flaw caused by the rendezvous radar
interface; in flight, the hardware stole \(15\%\) of all memory cycles,
triggering the famous 1202 and 1201 alarm conditions.\sidenote{\footnotesize During
  Apollo 11's lunar descent, asynchronous radar pulses flooded the AGC
  with unbudgeted interrupts, stealing \(15\%\) of CPU cycles and
  triggering 1202 alarms. The lander survived because priority-scheduled
  core memory dropped low-priority display tasks to maintain thruster
  cycles.} An even simpler failure mode on modern test benches occurs
when an injected overpressure fault triggers an unmonitored thermal
breaker or an auxiliary ground loop that drops power to the valve drive
coil. The valve springs shut mechanically, keeping pressure inside the
containment bound, while the software enforcer has actually deadlocked
in a priority inversion. An automated oracle that only inspects
downstream pressure registers a pass, manufacturing false confidence
from an unverified hardware artifact. The test framework must verify
that the specific enforcer path described in the safety claim executed
the corrective action.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-incidentux2a-15.5}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-incident}{Landmark Engineering Incident:}{Toyota Unintended Acceleration Bit-Flip \& Watchdog Death}
\phantomsection\label{callout-incident*-15.5}

\emph{System:} Toyota Electronic Throttle Control System (ETCS-i)
operating on an integrated Denso/Hitachi 32-bit microcontroller without
a hardware Memory Protection Unit (MPU) or task-isolated memory spaces
(\citeproc{ref-barr2013toyota}{Barr 2013};
\citeproc{ref-nasa2011toyota}{National Aeronautics and Space
Administration Engineering and Safety Center 2011}).

\emph{Incident:} Widespread unintended acceleration events (notably
\emph{Bookout v. Toyota}, 2007 Camry) resulting in catastrophic
high-speed collisions. Vehicles accelerated to wide-open throttle (WOT)
uncommanded; pumping or standing on the mechanical brake pedal was
insufficient to overcome full engine torque, and the throttle actuator
refused to close.

\emph{Root cause \& physics of failure:} Cosmic-ray Single-Event Upsets
(SEUs) or unhandled stack memory overwrites corrupted the Task Control
Block (TCB) and operating system stack pointers for the critical
real-time throttle control task (\texttt{Task\_Throttle}). The
corruption caused \texttt{Task\_Throttle} to terminate or hang in an
infinite loop, freezing its last commanded throttle angle at \(100\%\)
open. Crucially, the hardware watchdog timer was designed with a
catastrophic architectural flaw: it was kicked not by verifying the
deterministic execution and deadline compliance of
\texttt{Task\_Throttle}, but unconditionally by an asynchronous
background OS monitor task (\texttt{Task\_Monitor}). Because
\texttt{Task\_Monitor} continued running normally, the watchdog timer
never timed out and never asserted a hardware system reset.\sidenote{\footnotesize Forensic
  analysis in \emph{Bookout v. Toyota} (2013) revealed unbounded stack
  growth and a fatal architectural flaw: the hardware watchdog timer was
  refreshed by an asynchronous OS monitor task that continued executing
  after the primary throttle control task had died.} Furthermore,
because the failsafe task shared global memory variables without memory
protection, it too suffered memory corruption and failed to engage the
throttle fail-safe return spring.

\emph{Systems resolution:} Enforce strict spatial memory isolation via
hardware MPUs/MMUs; decouple safety reflexes onto an independent
real-time microcontroller (the Dual-Brain architecture); implement
windowed hardware watchdogs that require deadman tokens from
\emph{every} active hard real-time task; and hardwire independent
brake-override logic directly into power stage gate drivers.

\emph{Systems takeaway:} A software watchdog that monitors overall CPU
execution rather than individual task invariants is a fatal
architectural illusion: a dead control task can leave actuators locked
at maximum destructive power while the watchdog continues reporting
nominal health.

\end{fbxSimple}

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-ruleux2a-15.6}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-rule}{Architect’s Rule of Thumb:}{The Watchdog Liveness Invariant}
\phantomsection\label{callout-rule*-15.6}

A software watchdog timer that monitors only overall CPU execution
verifies merely that silicon has electrical power; safety requires
independent windowed watchdogs that verify the deterministic execution
cadence and invariant assertions of every individual critical task.

\end{fbxSimple}

The intervention mechanism must be subjected to fault injection under
the exact operational conditions that make intervention necessary. A
safety enforcer that takes over cleanly when the system sits idle on a
test bench provides no evidence of safety in production. During an
operational crisis, the learned policy is typically running at maximum
computational throughput, memory buses are saturated with
high-resolution sensory streams, direct memory access channels are
transferring frame buffers, and the actuator is experiencing maximum
hydrodynamic load. The test framework must inject faults while the
processor is under peak thermal and electrical stress, verifying that
the hardware multiplexer can preempt the proposal path, flush the
command buffers, and assert control over the valve driver within the
\(P_{99}\) deadline of \(2.0\text{ ms}\)
(Figure~\ref{fig-15-hardware-fault-injection}). If the intervention path
shares an internal bus arbiter with the neural accelerator, the hardware
takeover can stall behind an un-preemptible burst transfer. A machine
whose safety case assumes instantaneous takeover will fail in the field
if that takeover was only ever verified on a quiet bus.

The complete deterministic protocol for conducting automated
hardware-in-the-loop fault injection, verifying real-time detection
invariants, and evaluating quantitative Signal Temporal Logic robustness
on target silicon is formalized below:

\subsection{Automated Hardware-in-the-Loop Fault Injection
Protocol}\label{automated-hardware-in-the-loop-fault-injection-protocol}

\textbf{Substrate \& Invariants:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Execution Substrate:} Hard real-time FPGA plant rig and testbed
  orchestrator (\(f = 1000\text{ Hz}\), hardware timestamping jitter
  \(< 500\text{ ns}\)).
\item
  \emph{Memory Invariant:} Pre-allocated static DMA buffers in host test
  orchestrator; zero runtime dynamic heap allocation on safety MCU.
\item
  \emph{Safety Interlock Authority:} Independent optical/laser truth
  sensors wired to hardware crowbar relays capable of cutting target
  actuator power within \(2.0\text{ ms}\) upon physical envelope breach.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Execution protocol:}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Pre-Execution Invariant \& Envelope Precondition Audit (Stage
  1):} Sample baseline environmental sensors via
  \(\mathcal{I}_{\text{truth}}\) (ambient temperature
  \(T_{\text{amb}}\), supply rail voltage \(V_{\text{bus}}\), baseline
  fluid pressure \(P_0\)). Verify environmental vector matches declared
  operating point:
  \(\|\mathbf{w}_{\text{meas}} - \mathbf{w}_{\text{env}}\| \le \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\text{env}}\).
  If preconditions are violated, log
  \texttt{ERR\_PRECONDITION\_OUT\_OF\_SPEC}, set
  \(\text{Verdict} \leftarrow \text{INVALID\_PRECONDITION}\), and abort.
\item
  \textbf{Baseline Closed-Loop Synchronization \& Steady-State Arming
  (Stage 2):} Arm FPGA plant simulator and power up target Dual-Brain
  SoC; initiate periodic control loop (\(1000\text{ Hz}\)). Establish
  synchronized reference clock across logic analyzer, FPGA plant, and
  truth digitizers via \(10\text{ MHz}\) PXI clock. Allow physical plant
  state \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) to stabilize in nominal operating envelope for
  \(t_{\text{settle}} = 2.000\text{ s}\). If baseline tracking error
  \(\|e_{\text{track}}\| > \epsilon_{\text{nom}}\), assert
  \texttt{ERR\_BENCH\_INSTABILITY}, set
  \(\text{Verdict} \leftarrow \text{INVALID\_PRECONDITION}\), and abort.
\item
  \textbf{Deterministic In-Situ Fault Injection Trigger (Stage 3):} At
  monotonic test epoch \(t_{\text{inject}}\), hardware test orchestrator
  asserts trigger line to inline injection rig:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \emph{Sensor Latency/Bias:} FPGA interceptor latches ADC register or
    holds stale CAN payload while preserving valid hardware timestamp.
  \item
    \emph{Bus Contention / Frame Stuffing:} Fieldbus disturbance node
    floods CAN bus with dominant identifier bits (\(98\%\) bus load).
  \item
    \emph{Power Rail Droop:} Programmable electronic load pulls
    \(V_{\text{core}}\) down from \(1.10\text{ V}\) to \(0.82\text{ V}\)
    for \(\Delta t_{\text{duration}} = 5.0\text{ ms}\).
  \item
    \emph{Actuator Mechanical Stall:} 4-quadrant dynamometer applies
    step counter-torque
    \(\tau_{\text{stall}} = 3.5 \times \tau_{\text{rated}}\). Record
    microsecond injection timestamp
    \(t_{\text{fault\_start}} \leftarrow t_{\text{now}}\).
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Real-Time Safety Enforcer Response \& Takeover Audit (Stage
  4):} Monitor target MCU safety enforcer pins, CAN bus telemetry, and
  gate-driver PWM lines via isolated logic analyzer:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    Detect assertion of Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) / diagnostic flag:
    \(t_{\text{det}} \leftarrow t_{\text{now}} \implies \Delta t_{\text{det}} = t_{\text{det}} - t_{\text{fault\_start}}\).
  \item
    Detect hardware multiplexer preemption of motor driver:
    \(t_{\text{takeover}} \leftarrow t_{\text{now}} \implies \Delta t_{\text{takeover}} = t_{\text{takeover}} - t_{\text{fault\_start}}\).
  \item
    Detect physical plant transition to safe bounded regime:
    \(t_{\text{bounded}} \leftarrow t_{\text{now}} \implies \Delta t_{\text{bounded}} = t_{\text{bounded}} - t_{\text{fault\_start}}\).
    If external containment rig trips due to structural envelope breach:
    hardware crowbar cuts actuator power; assert
    \texttt{ERR\_PHYSICAL\_BREACH}.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{Quantitative STL Robustness Evaluation \& Ledger Serialization
  (Stage 5):} Ingest continuous truth trajectory
  \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{obs}}(t)\) from independent instrumentation
  \(\mathcal{I}_{\text{truth}}\) over \(t \in [0, T_{\text{trial}}]\).
  Check telemetry integrity; if truth frames were dropped or DMA buffers
  overflowed, set
  \(\text{Verdict} \leftarrow \text{UNOBSERVABLE\_TELEMETRY}\),
  serialize partial trace, and return. Compute quantitative Signal
  Temporal Logic robustness:
  \[\rho^* = \rho(\phi_{\text{safe}}, \mathbf{x}_{\text{obs}}, 0).\] If
  \(\rho^* > 0\), \(\Delta t_{\text{det}} \le \tau_{\text{det\_max}}\),
  and \(\Delta t_{\text{takeover}} \le \tau_{\text{takeover\_max}}\),
  set \(\text{Verdict} \leftarrow \text{PASS}\); else set
  \(\text{Verdict} \leftarrow \text{FAIL}\). Assemble immutable
  \texttt{FaultExecutionRecord\_t} record, sign with Ed25519 hardware
  key, append to machine notebook, and return.
\end{enumerate}

\section{The Fault Manifest}\label{sec-verification-15-7}

The machine notebook tracks components, software artifacts, and
execution traces under the provenance and versioning rules established
in Section~\ref{sec-nervous-4-10}. To document verification evidence,
the notebook requires an explicit data structure that binds every
injected fault directly to the claim it challenges. The \textbf{fault
record} records nine mandatory fields for each experimental trial,
comprising the safety claim under attack, the precise operating envelope
point, the injected fault magnitude and duration, the target hardware
and software build versions, the raw sensor and bus telemetry trace, the
primary detector that caught the anomaly, the measured intervention
response time, the final physical outcome, and any secondary hardware
anomalies. In an active flow regulator, for instance, a complete entry
records that safety claim C-04 (containment under upstream supply surge)
was attacked at an operating envelope point of \(350\text{ kPa}\) inlet
pressure and \(45^\circ\text{C}\) fluid temperature. The fault was an
analytical step command forcing a \(24\text{ V}\) override on the valve
driver for \(120\text{ ms}\), applied to controller firmware revision
3.4.1 running on board revision B. The primary detector was an
independent pressure-gradient monitor, the response took
\(1.8\text{ ms}\), the physical outcome was containment maintained below
\(380\text{ kPa}\), and no thermal breaker trips or bus retries
occurred.

A verification log that only records passes and failures creates an
incentive to discard corrupted experiments, which systematically biases
the resulting evidence. If an injected communication fault on the
controller bus corrupts the logging daemon or causes an external
digitizer to drop frames, the experiment is unobservable. If an
auxiliary ground-fault breaker cuts bench power before the safety
enforcer can evaluate the flow boundary, the experiment is invalid.
Treating an unobservable or invalid run as a failed test misidentifies
bench artifacts as machine defects, while treating it as an absent trial
silently discards the conditions under which telemetry failed. The
notebook therefore segregates invalid trials, unobservable trials, and
valid executions into distinct categories. Every trial that fails to
yield complete telemetry is logged as unobservable alongside the raw
partial buffer, ensuring that missing telemetry cannot artificially
inflate apparent test coverage. The binary memory layout and invariant
contracts governing this data structure are formalized in
Table~\ref{tbl-15-verification-manifest-schema}.

Reporting verification progress as a single aggregate percentage
obscures critical engineering vulnerabilities. A safety case cannot rely
on a summary metric stating that a machine survived ninety-eight percent
of five thousand fault trials if all five thousand injections were
conducted at room temperature on a quiescent memory bus. Coverage must
instead be reported across separate operational dimensions, including
functional safety requirements, physical envelope boundaries, physical
and logical injection sites, timing tails, hardware build revisions, and
multi-fault combinations. For a flow regulator, boundary coverage tracks
whether faults were injected at maximum fluid viscosity, minimum
back-pressure, and maximum pump ripple. Timing tail coverage isolates
injections targeting the \(P_{99}\) scheduling latency of the nervous
system and peak direct memory access utilization. A machine achieves
acceptable verification not when an average coverage index exceeds an
arbitrary threshold, but when the minimum coverage across every
individual dimension satisfies the requirements of the safety
case.\sidenote{\footnotesize ANSI/UL 4600 mandates goal-based safety cases linking
  claims to traceable evidence rather than raw operational hours.
  Similarly, ISO 26262-5 mandates hardware fault injection to verify
  ASIL D diagnostic coverage (Single-Point Fault Metric \(\ge 99\%\),
  Latent Fault Metric \(\ge 90\%\)).}

Interpreting repeated trials requires distinguishing between
deterministic execution and stochastic sampling. Repeating the exact
same deterministic fault script five hundred times on a digital test
bench yields no more information than running it once. If initial
conditions, processor register states, clock dividers, and input
sequences are fixed, identical deterministic software executes the
identical branch sequence every time. Repetition adds evidentiary value
only when sampling physical and computational distributions that exhibit
stochastic variance. In a physical flow loop, repeated trials sample
turbulent velocity fluctuations, asynchronous interrupt arrivals, bus
arbitration contention, and phase jitter between the high-frequency
sensor clock and the policy inference cycle. In these stochastic
regimes, repetition measures the spread and tail of the response-time
distribution rather than re-confirming a deterministic path.

When a stochastic trial runs \(n\) consecutive times without a single
safety violation, the count of zero-failure trials bounds the maximum
underlying failure probability \(p\) for that specific test
distribution.\sidenote{\footnotesize For zero-failure testing, standard Wald
  confidence intervals degenerate to zero width. The exact
  Clopper-Pearson interval yields
  \(p_{\text{upper}} = 1 - \alpha^{1/n}\), preventing asymptotic
  Gaussian approximations from understating catastrophic risk in
  rare-event tail distributions.} If each trial has an independent
failure probability \(p\), the probability of observing zero failures
across \(n\) independent trials is \((1 - p)^n\). To establish that the
failure probability is bounded above by \(p\) at a statistical
confidence level of \(1 - \alpha\), the probability of observing an
all-pass outcome by chance from an unsafe system must not exceed
\(\alpha\), yielding \((1 - p)^n \le \alpha\). Taking the natural
logarithm of both sides gives \(n \ln(1 - p) \le \ln(\alpha)\). For rare
failure rates where \(p \ll 1\), the first-order Taylor expansion
\(\ln(1 - p) \approx -p\) provides the standard engineering
approximation \(n \ge -\ln(\alpha) / p\). For an exact calculation to
bound the failure probability below one percent (\(p \le 0.01\)) at
ninety-five percent confidence (\(\alpha = 0.05\)), the inequality is
\((1 - 0.01)^n \le 0.05\). Taking logarithms produces
\(n \ge \ln(0.05) / \ln(0.99) \approx -2.9957 / -0.01005 \approx 298.07\),
which requires exactly \(299\) independent, zero-failure trials.

The statistical validity of this one-sided binomial bound depends
entirely on two physical assumptions, namely trial independence and
operational representativeness. Independence requires that the outcome
of trial \(k\) has no effect on trial \(k+1\). If repeated fault
injections cause resistive heating in a valve solenoid coil, increasing
coil resistance and slowing valve actuation across successive tests, the
trials are coupled by a hidden thermal state, and the binomial formula
is invalid. Representativeness requires that the test conditions
accurately reflect the true operational environment. Running 299
successful fault injections under steady, laminar flow at
\(20^\circ\text{C}\) proves that the failure probability is below one
percent at ninety-five percent confidence only for laminar flow at
\(20^\circ\text{C}\). It provides zero empirical or mathematical basis
for claiming safety during turbulent flow, severe cavitation, or
cold-start operations at \(-10^\circ\text{C}\).

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-mathux2a-15.7}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-math}{Fermi Math:}{Hardware Fault Injection Coverage and Mean Time Between Unmitigated Faults (MTBUF)}
\phantomsection\label{callout-math*-15.7}

\emph{Scenario:} An autonomous physical AI system operates with a
cumulative raw hardware component failure rate \(\lambda_{\text{raw}}\)
across its perception sensors, communication transceivers,
microcontrollers, and inverter gate drivers. We calculate the diagnostic
coverage \(C_{\text{diag}}\) that Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) fault
injection must empirically prove to achieve a target Mean Time Between
Unmitigated Faults (\(\text{MTBUF}\)) of \(10^7\text{ hours}\)
(equivalent to an unmitigated failure rate
\(\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}} \le 10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1} = 100\text{ FIT}\)),
and derive the required number of zero-failure HIL test trials
\(N_{\text{trials}}\).

\textbf{System Failure Rate \& Unmitigated Failure Relation:}
\[\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}} = \lambda_{\text{raw}} \cdot (1 - C_{\text{diag}}) \implies \text{MTBUF} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}}} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{raw}} (1 - C_{\text{diag}})}\]
Solving for required diagnostic coverage:
\[C_{\text{diag}} \ge 1 - \frac{\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}}}{\lambda_{\text{raw}}} = 1 - \frac{1}{\text{MTBUF} \cdot \lambda_{\text{raw}}}\]

\textbf{1. Cumulative Raw Hardware Failure Rate:} Suppose an embedded
computing and actuation stack incorporates:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  4 CMOS cameras + 2 LiDAR modules:
  \(\lambda_{\text{sensors}} = 6 \times 250\text{ FIT} = 1,500\text{ FIT}\)
\item
  2 Dual-Brain SoCs (Linux MPUs + Safety MCUs):
  \(\lambda_{\text{compute}} = 2 \times 500\text{ FIT} = 1,000\text{ FIT}\)
\item
  CAN/Ethernet Transceivers + Power Distribution PMICs:
  \(\lambda_{\text{bus/power}} = 2,500\text{ FIT}\)
\item
  6 Inverter Power Stages and Gate Drivers:
  \(\lambda_{\text{inverters}} = 6 \times 800\text{ FIT} = 4,800\text{ FIT}\)
\item
  Total raw hardware failure rate: \[\begin{aligned}
  \lambda_{\text{raw}} &= 1,500 + 1,000 + 2,500 + 4,800 = 9,800\text{ FIT} \\
  &= 9.8 \times 10^{-6}\text{ faults/h} \quad (\approx 1\text{ raw fault per } 102,000\text{ hours})
  \end{aligned}\]
\end{itemize}

\textbf{2. Required Diagnostic Coverage Calculation:} To guarantee an
unmitigated catastrophic failure rate
\(\lambda_{\text{unmitigated}} \le 10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}\)
(\(\text{MTBUF} \ge 10^7\text{ hours}\)):
\[C_{\text{diag}} \ge 1 - \frac{10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}}{9.8 \times 10^{-6}\text{ h}^{-1}} = 1 - 0.0102 = 0.9898 \implies C_{\text{diag}} \ge 99.0\%\]

\textbf{3. Required Statistical Zero-Failure HIL Test Count:} Using the
exact Clopper-Pearson binomial tail bound at \(95\%\) confidence
(\(\alpha = 0.05\)): \[\begin{aligned}
(1 - p_{\text{unmitigated}})^N &\le \alpha \implies N_{\text{trials}} \ge \frac{\ln(\alpha)}{\ln(C_{\text{diag}})} \\
&= \frac{\ln(0.05)}{\ln(0.990)} \approx \frac{-2.9957}{-0.01005} \approx 298.1 \implies 299\text{ trials}
\end{aligned}\] If safety integrity escalates to ASIL D
(\(C_{\text{diag}} \ge 99.9\%\), \(p_{\text{unmitigated}} \le 0.001\)):
\[N_{\text{trials}} \ge \frac{-\ln(0.05)}{1 - 0.999} = \frac{2.9957}{0.001} \approx 2,996\text{ consecutive zero-failure HIL injection trials}\]

\emph{Archetype coverage comparison:}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Mobile System (Autonomous Ground Transport):} Total raw rate
  \(\lambda_{\text{raw}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ h}^{-1}\); targeting
  ASIL D unmitigated rate (\(10^{-8}\text{ h}^{-1}\)) requires
  \(C_{\text{diag}} \ge 99.92\%\), demanding \(3,745\) zero-failure HIL
  brake/steer brownout injections.
\item
  \emph{Manipulator (6-DoF Articulated Arm):} Raw joint inverter rate
  \(\lambda_{\text{raw}} = 6.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ h}^{-1}\); targeting
  SIL 3 (\(10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}\)) requires
  \(C_{\text{diag}} \ge 98.33\%\), requiring \(179\) zero-failure
  joint-stall brake clamp trials.
\item
  \emph{Process System (High-Pressure Flow Regulator):} Raw
  transducer/valve rate
  \(\lambda_{\text{raw}} = 8.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ h}^{-1}\); targeting
  \(10^{-7}\text{ h}^{-1}\) requires \(C_{\text{diag}} \ge 98.82\%\),
  demanding \(253\) zero-failure cavitation/stale-pressure injection
  trials.
\end{itemize}

\end{fbxSimple}

When target reliability requirements scale from advisory levels to
life-critical integrity levels, the sample size required by binomial and
exponential tail bounds becomes physically impossible to achieve through
black-box operational exposure alone. This fundamental
limitation---formalized by Butler and Finelli
(\citeproc{ref-butler1993infeasibility}{Butler and Finelli 1993}) as the
\textbf{Butler \& Finelli Infeasibility Bound}---dictates that
certifying ultra-high cyber-physical reliability (e.g., \(10^{-9}\)
catastrophic failures per hour) through unperturbed operational exposure
alone is physically impossible due to astronomical time requirements
(e.g., \(>3.0 \times 10^9\text{ hours}\) of continuous zero-failure
testing), mathematically necessitating deterministic fault injection,
layered runtime invariant enforcement, and formal architectural
partitioning.

As quantified in Table~\ref{tbl-15-statistical-testing-bounds},
certifying an avionics DAL A or ISO 26262 ASIL D catastrophic failure
rate of \(10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}\) at \(95\%\) confidence requires over
\(3.0 \times 10^9\text{ hours}\) (more than 342,000 years) of
continuous, zero-failure physical operation. Even a distributed fleet of
100 dedicated test vehicles operating continuously 24 hours a day would
require over 3,400 years to establish this statistical claim.
Consequently, physical AI systems cannot be validated solely by
accumulating millions of unperturbed operational fleet miles; safety
assurance must instead be established through deterministic fault
injection, layered runtime invariant enforcement, and formal
architectural partitioning.

\(10^6\text{ h}\))} & \(p \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-12}\) &
\(3.0 \times 10^6\text{ h}\) & \(3.0 \times 10^6\text{ h}\)\emph{(342
years continuous)} & \(3.4\text{ years}\)\emph{(at 24/7 continuous
operation)} & \textbf{Hybrid Verification:} Statistical sampling paired
with accelerated fault injection and HIL parameter stress sweeps. \\
\textbf{Automotive Safety (ASIL D / SIL 3)}\emph{(ISO 26262 / IEC
61508)} & \(10^{-8}\text{ h}^{-1}\)\emph{(10 FIT / \(10^8\text{ h}\))} &
\(p \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-14}\) & \(3.0 \times 10^8\text{ h}\) &
\(3.0 \times 10^8\text{ h}\)\emph{(34,200 years continuous)} &
\(342\text{ years}\)\emph{(100 vehicles 24/7)} & \textbf{Architectural
Containment Mandatory:} Formal invariant synthesis, hardware interlocks,
and systematic fault injection; fleet testing cannot prove safety. \\
\textbf{Life-Critical Avionics (DAL A / SIL 4)}\emph{(DO-178C / FAA AC
20-115D)} & \(10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}\)\emph{(1 failure /
\(10^9\text{ h}\))} & \(p \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-15}\) &
\(3.0 \times 10^9\text{ h}\) &
\(3.0 \times 10^9\text{ h}\)\emph{(342,465 years continuous)} &
\(3,425\text{ years}\)\emph{(100 units 24/7 continuous)} &
\textbf{Mathematical Impossibility of Black-Box Test:} Safety
\emph{cannot} be established by fleet exposure. Provenance, formal
methods, and isolated intervention are mathematically required. \\
\end{longtable}

A defensible safety case requires that untested operational envelopes,
unobservable test results, and unsupported probability claims be
presented with the exact same visual and structural prominence as
successful verifications. Hiding an untested envelope boundary or an
unverified hardware permutation in an appendix manufactures a false
impression of completeness. The fault record must explicitly list every
parameter combination where fault injection was omitted due to test
bench limitations, sensor bandwidth constraints, or destructive hardware
limits. Documenting what was never tested prevents unverified
operational zones from silently masquerading as verified safety margins
when the record is transferred to the safety case in
Chapter~\ref{sec-release}. Furthermore, every isolated entry in the
record documents the response of the machine to a single, localized
disturbance. In physical operation, however, disturbances rarely occur
in strict isolation, and verifying how a machine responds to an
individual fault leaves open the question of how it behaves when
multiple nominal disturbances strike the system at the same time.

\section{Systems Stress-Tests}\label{sec-verification-15-8}

A machine that passes every isolated fault injection test can fail when
two nominal disturbances occur at the same time. If a system possesses
\(N\) cataloged failure modes, testing every arbitrary pair requires
\(\mathcal{O}(N^2)\) injection trials, and higher-order combinations
expand exponentially. Exhaustive combinatorial injection is physically
intractable, and unguided random sampling wastes testing resources on
independent components that share no physical or logical connection.
Systems stress-testing avoids combinatorial explosion by deriving
compound fault vectors directly from shared physical resources, common
electrical paths, cascading detector dependencies, and latency budgets
that accumulate across handoffs. The following four analytical
stress-tests evaluate machines where individually compliant subsystems
combine into catastrophic physical failures:

\subsection*{Stress-Test 1: Compound Latency Accumulation across
Distributed
Handoffs}\label{stress-test-1-compound-latency-accumulation-across-distributed-handoffs}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 1: Compound Latency
Accumulation across Distributed Handoffs}

\emph{The scenario.} An industrial liquid-propellant flow regulator
(\(P_{\text{inlet}} = 12.0\text{ MPa}\), nominal flow
\(15.0\text{ kg/s}\)) requires flow transients to be arrested within an
end-to-end deadline of \(250.0\text{ ms}\) to prevent chamber rupture at
\(14.5\text{ MPa}\). Execution is distributed across three nodes on a
shared \(10\text{ Mbps}\) CAN bus: an optical densitometer (ingest
budget \(80.0\text{ ms}\)), a GPU inference node (execution budget
\(120.0\text{ ms}\)), and a valve actuator node (budget
\(40.0\text{ ms}\)). In standalone tests, sensor delay
(\(75.0\text{ ms}\)), inference delay (\(115.0\text{ ms}\)), and valve
delay (\(38.0\text{ ms}\)) all pass local watchdog limits.

\emph{The systems dilemma.} When an upstream cavitation surge occurs,
sensor, planner, and actuator simultaneously experience their worst-case
individually compliant delays, while unthrottled diagnostic logging adds
\(45.0\text{ ms}\) of bus queuing. Total cumulative latency reaches
\(75.0\text{ ms} + 115.0\text{ ms} + 38.0\text{ ms} + 45.0\text{ ms} = 273.0\text{ ms}\),
exceeding the \(250.0\text{ ms}\) physical vessel limit by
\(23.0\text{ ms}\) and bursting the vessel while every local watchdog
reports nominal health.

\emph{The systems verdict: Additive Timing Composition Law.} Local
watchdog timers are mathematically incapable of guaranteeing end-to-end
physical safety when handoff delays accumulate. Verification must
enforce distributed end-to-end deadline tracking rather than isolated
component timeouts.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 2: Shared Bus Saturation and Control Loop
Starvation}\label{stress-test-2-shared-bus-saturation-and-control-loop-starvation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 2: Shared Bus Saturation
and Control Loop Starvation}

\emph{The scenario.} An autonomous platform coordinates sensing, neural
inference, safety reflexes, and evidence logging across a single shared
field bus. An unthrottled diagnostic flight-recorder memory dump pushes
bus utilization to \(98\%\).

\emph{The systems dilemma.} Bus contention does not produce an isolated
delay in a single subsystem; it simultaneously delays raw sensor packets
to the planner, setpoints to valve actuators, heartbeats to the safety
enforcer, and crash logs to the evidence ledger. The simultaneous loss
of actuator commands and enforcement telemetry starves the safety loop,
preventing the monitor from detecting an actuator freeze.

\emph{The systems verdict: Shared Interconnect Contention Invariant.}
Common communication media couple previously independent subsystems
during transients. Critical safety heartbeats and actuator telemetry
must reside on isolated physical channels or hardware-prioritized
time-triggered slots.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 3: Asymmetric Detector Dependency under Supply
Transients}\label{stress-test-3-asymmetric-detector-dependency-under-supply-transients}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 3: Asymmetric Detector
Dependency under Supply Transients}

\emph{The scenario.} A power supply ripple causes an optical flow meter
to experience a digital register freeze, latching output telemetry at a
steady nominal \(4.2\text{ kg/s}\). Concurrently, a mechanical valve
blockage restricts physical flow to \(0.8\text{ kg/s}\).

\emph{The systems dilemma.} Because the latched value
(\(4.2\text{ kg/s}\)) falls within nominal bounds and generates no
framing errors, the anomaly detector never flags a fault. The neural
planner reads nominal flow and issues no corrective command, preventing
the safety enforcer from opening the auxiliary relief line. Testing the
blockage alone or the sensor freeze alone passes; only the compound test
exposes the disabled detector.

\emph{The systems verdict: Asymmetric Detector Dependency Law.} A
primary electrical fault can disable the exact sensory detector required
to contain a secondary mechanical failure. Verification must audit the
causal graph to ensure safety monitors rely on physically independent,
cross-modal transducers.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 4: Unobservable Trial Outcomes under Diagnostic
Reset}\label{stress-test-4-unobservable-trial-outcomes-under-diagnostic-reset}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 4: Unobservable Trial
Outcomes under Diagnostic Reset}

\emph{The scenario.} During an aggressive multi-fault injection test on
high-speed motion hardware, bus contention causes the testbench data
logger to drop packets, and an emergency watchdog reset wipes volatile
diagnostic trace RAM.

\emph{The systems dilemma.} Because the recording apparatus failed, the
physical trajectory, peak reaction forces, and timing margins throughout
the transient cannot be reconstructed. The test team attempts to score
the trial as a ``pass'' because the physical machine did not strike
mechanical stops.

\emph{The systems verdict: Unobservable Trial Invalidation Law.} An
unobservable outcome is an invalid test and an instrumentation defect,
never evidence that the machine survived. If the testbed cannot
deterministically measure state throughout a fault transient, the run
yields zero evidentiary value.

\section{Summary}\label{sec-verification-15-9}

A demonstration shows that a machine can function under favorable
circumstances, while verification generates structured evidence that a
design claim holds when those circumstances fail. In an analytical
example of an industrial flow regulator, allowing an observer to watch
an automated control loop maintain line pressure at \(4.0\text{ MPa}\)
across three uninterrupted operating shifts proves only that the nominal
trajectory did not encounter an unhandled disturbance. It does not
establish what happens when a proportional relief valve jams at \(15\%\)
travel during a sudden pump surge, or whether the pressure transducer's
degraded bandwidth violates the intervention deadline. A demonstration
produces confidence, which is psychological and decays with the first
unexpected physical transient. Verification produces evidence, which is
an auditable record of bounded claims tested against deliberate physical
and computational stress. Downstream systems and safety cases receive
this concrete evidence rather than subjective confidence.

The operating envelope defines the physical boundary within which safety
claims are made, evaluated, and reproduced. Outside this envelope,
physical dynamics deviate from the models used during design, turning
test results into uninterpretable noise. Inside it, every parameter
boundary corresponds to a specific physical constraint, such as an inlet
fluid velocity ceiling of \(6.0\text{ m/s}\) or an ambient temperature
limit of \(65.0^\circ\text{C}\). When a stress-test injects an upstream
pressure surge of \(1.5\text{ MPa/s}\) into the regulator, the test is
meaningful only because the design explicitly claimed stability across
pressure derivatives up to \(2.0\text{ MPa/s}\). If a test exposes a
pressure overshoot exceeding the \(5.0\text{ MPa}\) structural vessel
limit while operating within this boundary, the failure is reproducible
and falsifies the design claim. If an identical pressure overshoot
occurs only after the fluid velocity exceeds \(9.0\text{ m/s}\), the
failure indicates that the test apparatus breached the operating
envelope, measuring physics that the controller was never budgeted to
reject.

Verification derives its structure from the properties established
across the preceding design stages. Every contract stated in the
pipeline becomes an explicit fault waiting to be injected into the
assembled machine. For the flow regulator, the design claims from
earlier chapters dictate a strict chain of traceability. A sensor
calibration claim from the perception pipeline becomes an injected drift
fault of \(0.2\text{ MPa}\), testing whether the diagnostic estimator
detects the discrepancy before flow estimation errors propagate to the
policy. A policy latency claim of \(115\text{ ms}\) at \(P_{99}\)
becomes an injected inference jitter fault, verifying that the nervous
system detects the schedule overrun and executes an immediate fallback
trajectory. An actuator authority claim becomes an injected valve slew
saturation fault, confirming that the mechanical intervention mechanism
isolates the line within the \(250\text{ ms}\) physical vessel budget.
Each verification vector links five distinct elements in an unbroken
chain, connecting the original design property, the injected
disturbance, the runtime detector, the nervous system response, and the
final measured physical state.

Every qualification mode operates under explicit evidentiary limits.
Hardware-in-the-loop simulation permits dense sampling of rare boundary
crossings, running thousands of synthetic cavitation transients without
wearing out physical seals, but it remains blind to unmodeled
hydrodynamic turbulence and bus transceiver heating. Physical
dynamometer testing captures true thermal dissipation, electromagnetic
interference, and mechanical backlash, but it cannot safely execute
destructive overpressurization tests to failure across hundreds of
consecutive runs. Treating a simulated pass as proof of physical
compliance confuses the fidelity of a model with physical reality.
Conversely, treating a physical test under a single ambient condition as
a universal guarantee ignores environmental coupling. Any operating
condition, input distribution, or hardware degradation state that has
not been subjected to deliberate fault injection remains an open claim
rather than an established property.

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-takeawaysux2a-15.8}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-takeaways}{Key Chapter Takeaways}{}
\phantomsection\label{callout-takeaways*-15.8}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Demonstrations Build Psychological Confidence; Verification
  Generates Auditable Evidence:} Watching a machine run without failure
  proves only that nominal conditions held. Verification requires
  deliberate physical fault injection across boundary envelopes to prove
  that safety invariants hold when subsystems fail.
\item
  \textbf{Local Watchdogs Cannot Prevent Additive Timing Failure:} If
  sensor (\(75\text{ ms}\)), GPU inference (\(115\text{ ms}\)), valve
  actuator (\(38\text{ ms}\)), and diagnostic logging (\(45\text{ ms}\))
  all operate within local limits, their sum (\(273\text{ ms}\))
  breaches the physical vessel limit (\(250\text{ ms}\)). Safety
  verification must track end-to-end distributed deadline accumulation.
\item
  \textbf{Compound Fault Vectors Must Trace Shared Physical Resources:}
  Testing single faults in isolation misses catastrophic interactions.
  Electrical voltage ripples can freeze digital register outputs at
  nominal values, disabling the exact software anomaly detector needed
  to catch a concurrent mechanical valve jam.
\item
  \textbf{Unobservable Test Outcomes Yield Zero Evidentiary Value:} If
  testbed data loggers drop packets or watchdog resets wipe diagnostic
  trace RAM during a fault transient, the run is an invalid test, never
  evidence that the machine survived the fault.
\item
  \textbf{The Versioned Fault Record is the Sole Prerequisite for
  Release:} The output of verification is an immutable fault record
  cataloging verified passes, hard failures, invalid runs, and explicit
  coverage gaps handed directly to the release assurance safety case.
\end{itemize}

\end{fbxSimple}

The output of this verification process is a versioned fault record
delivered directly to the safety case assembled in
Chapter~\ref{sec-release}. This record documents the outcome of every
injected vector without aggregation or statistical smoothing. It details
the verified passes where measured bounds held with quantifiable
margins, the hard failures where detection or intervention deadlines
were missed, and the invalid tests where testbed artifacts or envelope
violations corrupted the data. It highlights the remaining coverage gaps
where test vectors could not be safely or physically executed, and it
explicitly flags unsupported probability claims where rare-event tail
distributions were estimated without sufficient sample depth.
Chapter~\ref{sec-release} builds the formal assurance argument that
justifies operating the machine, converting the fault record into
bounded claims for release. When those physical evidence bounds confront
the open-world distribution shift and rare, unmodeled hazards of
deployment, Chapter~\ref{sec-frontier} synthesizes the overarching
epistemic boundary of physical AI, establishing how runtime systems
enforce safety even when verification reaches its fundamental limits.

\chapter{\texorpdfstring{Deployment Release \& Safety
Cases\chaptersubtitle{Deciding Whether It Should Operate}}{Deployment Release \& Safety Cases}}\label{sec-release}

\emph{Under what auditable chain of physical evidence is an autonomous
machine permitted to move among humans?}

Deploying a physical AI system into human environments is an accountable
engineering decision requiring auditable evidence rather than
statistical optimism. Whether releasing an autonomous mobile
transporter, a collaborative robot arm, or a continuous chemical
reactor, a safety case cannot rely on benchmark accuracy. It demands a
structured Claim-Argument-Evidence tree connecting every operational
claim to reproducible hardware measurements and deterministic bounds. A
defensible verdict defines an explicit operational design domain,
deploys real-time monitors for distribution shift, and specifies strict
triggers that revoke operating authority the moment physical assumptions
fail.

\newpage{}

\protect\phantomsection\label{callout-objectiveux2a-16.1}
\begin{fbxSimple}{callout-objective}{Learning Objectives}{}
\phantomsection\label{callout-objective*-16.1}

After studying this section, you will be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Assemble a claim, an argument, and the evidence supporting each link
  across physical machine archetypes.
\item
  Trace every condition in a verdict back to a calibrated sensor
  measurement, physical force limit, or timing bound.
\item
  Render operate, operate-with-conditions, or do not operate verdicts,
  and state what each obliges during subsequent deployment.
\item
  Attack an argument you wrote using adversarial red-team probes and
  identify its weakest link.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Core physical AI insight.} A verdict is an argument from evidence
to a claim, and it is only as strong as its weakest link. Physical AI
systems are never `generally safe'; operating authority is a decaying
cryptographic lease strictly conditioned on bounded ODD evidence.
Release is an accountable systems decision rather than another benchmark
test, and what it decides is one machine, inside a stated envelope, for
a stated period.

\end{fbxSimple}

\section{The Decision to Deploy}\label{sec-release-16-1}

\lettrine{E}{very design choice}\lettrine{,}{} latency budget, fallback
reflex, and fault injection test recorded across the preceding systems
architecture layers was built to withstand physical reality. But
physical reality does not inspect logs or grant operating authority. At
some point, the development phase concludes, the engineering team
prepares to hand the machine over to its operators, and an engineer must
sign a statement asserting that the machine is fit to operate. As
highlighted in the nervous system organ locator
(Figure~\ref{fig-locator}), everything the engineering team has
measured, bounded, and verified across the body, the nervous system, the
learned policy, and the runtime architecture must now be compiled into
an explicit, traceable argument that an adversarial auditor could
attempt to dismantle. The strength of that argument dictates whether the
machine is allowed to draw power, move its joints, and interact with the
physical world outside the laboratory.

Release introduces no new physical mechanisms, adds no fallback
controllers, and retrains no neural weights. It is an act of systems
adjudication over existing evidence. Until this point, engineering
effort was directed at creating capabilities and bounding their hazards.
Engineers budgeted sensor jitter on the communication bus, measured tail
latencies under distributions such as \(P_{99.9}\), implemented watchdog
timers to preempt frozen inference pipelines, and characterized
behavioral stability when the policy encounters unfamiliar physical
contact. The release process does not alter any of these measurements.
Instead, it aggregates the disparate verification artifacts (timing
logs, hardware stress tests, empirical fault rates, and formal
containment proofs) into a connected argument graph. The graph links
low-level evidence to a high-level operational claim. If the evidence is
sound, and if the assumptions regarding the operating environment remain
valid, the machine satisfies its safety envelope. If any single link in
that chain fails under inspection, the entire claim collapses.

A release verdict is not a prediction of future perfection, nor is it a
statistical guarantee that a machine will never encounter an unhandled
condition. A learned model deployed in an unconstrained physical
environment cannot be proven correct in the sense of a mathematical
theorem. Instead, the release verdict functions as an explicit, bounded
contract between an operational claim, empirical evidence, and runtime
enforcement. The operational claim defines precisely what the machine is
authorized to do, the specific physical environment in which it is
permitted to act, and the exact time interval over which the
authorization remains valid. The empirical evidence demonstrates that
the learned brain acts within acceptable behavioral envelopes during
nominal operations. When the learned model inevitably makes an error,
runtime enforcement guarantees that the deterministic nervous system
detects the transgression and forces the body into a safe state before
kinetic energy, thermal dissipation, or mechanical stress exceeds
tolerable limits.

Adjudication evaluates the compiled evidence against the operational
claim and produces one of three distinct verdicts, designated as
\textbf{Operate}, \textbf{Operate with Conditions}, and \textbf{Do Not
Operate}. A verdict of operate grants full authorization within the
requested envelope, certifying that every link in the argument graph is
supported by verified data. A verdict of operate with conditions grants
restricted authorization, narrowing the operating envelope to match the
limits of the evidence. For instance, the adjudicator might reduce
maximum allowable end-effector velocity from \(1.5\text{ m/s}\) to
\(0.5\text{ m/s}\), mandate a physical barrier between the workspace and
human personnel, or shorten the mandatory sensor recalibration interval
from thirty days to seven. A verdict of do not operate denies
authorization entirely. In traditional software engineering, refusing to
deploy code is often viewed as a scheduling failure or a lost release
cycle. In physical AI, where an uncontained failure exerts physical work
against the world, refusal is a successful engineering outcome. The
safety case functioned correctly by identifying an unsupported claim
before the machine could cause physical harm.

The rigor of this adjudication becomes clear when applied to a concrete
physical system. Throughout this text, the release process is grounded
in an autonomous tactile manipulation cell designed to sort, finish, and
transfer heavy metal castings on an active manufacturing line. The
machine comprises an articulated arm capable of exerting
\(450\text{ N}\) of grip force, carrying a \(12\text{ kg}\) payload at
velocities up to \(1.8\text{ m/s}\), and interacting directly with human
assembly workers during part handovers. The primary operational claim
asserts that the cell will perform its sorting and finishing tasks
without exceeding \(50\text{ N}\) of transient contact force against a
human worker, even during unpredicted collisions, model stalls, or
sudden power interruptions.

Establishing that claim requires an unbroken evidentiary chain. The
adjudicator must verify that the low-level tactile reflex executes at
\(1000\text{ Hz}\) with a deterministic worst-case latency of
\(P_{99.99} \le 1.8\text{ ms}\), that the motor drives physically cut
drive current within \(15\text{ ms}\) of a threshold violation, and that
the vision-language-action policy cannot command a joint trajectory
outside the mechanical work envelope even when visual sensing is
degraded by dust or fluctuating illumination. If the vision pipeline
exhibits a \(240\text{ ms}\) tail stall that delays object detection, or
if thermal buildup in the actuator windings alters torque delivery over
a four-hour operating shift, the argument fails. Adjudication strips
away optimism, replacing informal confidence with an auditable record of
who measured each quantity, what instrumentation was used, and who
accepts formal accountability for the verdict.

\section{The Release Question}\label{sec-release-16-2}

Deciding whether a physical machine should operate is fundamentally
different from evaluating the statistical performance of a model or
witnessing a successful laboratory demonstration. High validation
accuracy on an offline dataset demonstrates only that a learned policy
can reproduce training correlations under stationary data distributions.
Similarly, a flawless live demonstration shows only that one specific
sequence of states executed without failure under the particular
environmental conditions present during that test run. Neither result
answers the release question. The engineering release question asks
whether the accumulated evidence justifies delegating physical authority
over mass, force, and velocity to an autonomous system under a defined
set of operating conditions. A physical AI system does not merely
produce informational outputs that a human supervisor can review and
discard. It converts computational outputs into mechanical work against
physical objects and human bodies. When authority is granted to a
learned policy whose internal representations are unaccountable, release
is the formal engineering decision to permit that policy to actuate the
hardware because deterministic safeguards guarantee that the machine
remains within safe physical bounds under all single-point failures.

The boundaries of this delegation are formalized through the
\textbf{operational design domain}, defined as an explicit set of
measurable physical invariants. An \textbf{operational design domain
(ODD) invariant} represents a measurable physical, environmental, or
kinematic parameter boundary (such as payload mass, workspace volume,
friction coefficients, or thermal limits) within which a physical AI
system's learned policies and deterministic reflexes are certified to
maintain safe operation. In the tactile manipulation cell, these
invariants specify the geometric workspace volume as a hemisphere of
radius \(1.2\text{ m}\) centered at the arm base, payload mass between
\(0.5\text{ kg}\) and \(12.0\text{ kg}\), contact friction coefficients
satisfying \(\mu \ge 0.35\), ambient operating temperatures from
\(15^\circ\text{C}\) to \(40^\circ\text{C}\), ambient lighting between
\(300\text{ lx}\) and \(2000\text{ lx}\), and human co-presence states
restricted to a single trained operator within the collaborative
handover envelope.

Inside these boundaries lies the nominal operating zone where the
learned policy retains full authority. When environmental factors drift
toward the perimeter, such as illuminance dropping toward
\(200\text{ lx}\) or surface moisture reducing friction below
\(\mu = 0.35\), the system enters degraded conditional zones where
operating speeds are automatically curtailed or secondary sensor
modalities are engaged. Outside the boundary lies the hard refusal
envelope. If a sensor measurement violates any physical invariant, such
as detecting a \(15\text{ kg}\) payload or ambient heat exceeding
\(40^\circ\text{C}\), the nervous system revokes policy authority,
commands mechanical brakes, and prevents further operation. In heavy
autonomous fleets, such as the autonomous mining haul truck shown in
Figure~\ref{fig-16-real-autonomous-haul-truck}, this boundary
enforcement is multi-tiered: high-precision GNSS antennas and radio
telemetry masts enforce spatial geofencing within the pit corridor,
bumper radar and LiDAR pods detect foreign obstacles and dust
degradation, and dedicated safety controllers trip electro-hydraulic
service brakes the instant perimeter containment is lost.

\caption{\label{fig-16-real-autonomous-haul-truck}\textbf{Operational

240-metric-ton Caterpillar 793D autonomous mining haul truck operating
inside a strictly geofenced open-pit mine corridor. Heavy physical AI
systems operating with tens of megajoules of kinetic energy enforce
explicit, multi-layered ODD boundaries: centimeter-accurate dual GNSS
antenna masts and wireless telemetry on the cab roof enforce spatial
corridor geofencing; bumper-mounted radar and LiDAR sensor pods detect
foreign obstacles and dust/fog atmospheric degradation; and hardwired
emergency-stop tripwires de-energize electro-hydraulic steering and

MineStar System Field Trial Archive (Public Domain / Fair Use under 17
U.S.C. § 107).}

As formalized in Table~\ref{tbl-16-odd-invariants}, every physical
parameter governing the operational design domain must be partitioned
into three explicit subsets: nominal operating states
(\(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{nom}}\)), degraded conditional states
(\(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}\)), and hard refusal boundaries
(\(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}\)). Rather than treating environmental
boundaries as descriptive guidelines, the release contract couples each
physical invariant to a calibrated runtime sensor modality, a guaranteed
sampling period, and a deterministic hardware enforcer action. If any
environmental parameter drifts into \(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cond}}\), the
nervous system automatically clamps kinematic authority; if it
penetrates \(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{refuse}}\), operating authority is
immediately revoked before uncontained kinetic energy can accumulate.
