\section{Epistemic Governance and Operational
Limits}\label{sec-frontier-17-8}

The ultimate maturity of physical AI engineering lies in how an
organization governs the claims its empirical records cannot settle. In
digital software, unhandled edge cases are often treated as minor bugs
to be patched in subsequent agile sprints. In physical systems governing
moving mass, high voltages, or chemical flows, unhandled edge cases
cause permanent material fracture, thermal runaway, and loss of human
life. Statutory safety standards---such as ISO 26262 ASIL D, IEC 61508
SIL 3, and modern autonomous governance standards such as UL 4600 and
ISO 21448 (SOTIF)---explicitly require that unmonitored assumptions be
cataloged, bounded, and audited throughout the entire operational
lifecycle.\sidenote{\footnotesize While ISO 26262/IEC 61508 address hardware and
  software bugs, ISO 21448 (SOTIF) and UL 4600 mandate safety cases
  evaluating performance insufficiencies, sensor blind zones, and
  unknown edge cases, prohibiting deployment based on statistical
  extrapolation.}

When empirical fleet exposure cannot breach the Astronomical Exposure
Wall (\(n \ge \frac{\ln(1/\alpha)}{p}\)), the engineering team must
enforce four non-negotiable operational disciplines:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Permanent Residual Registers:} Epistemic blind spots are not
  temporary backlog items. Every entry in
  Table~\ref{tbl-17-claims-register} represents a permanent
  architectural constraint until an independent physical measurement or
  proven analytical invariant discharges it.
\item
  \textbf{Deterministic Nervous-System Primacy:} High-capacity neural
  policies running on application processors must never possess
  unmediated actuator write privileges. Actuator drive registers
  (\texttt{TIMx\_CCR}, \texttt{ePWM\ CMPA}) must be governed by
  bare-metal real-time microcontrollers executing deterministic safety
  filters with sub-millisecond reaction times.
\item
  \textbf{Passive Hardware Bounding:} Where observation latencies exceed
  the body's time-to-harm
  (\(\tau_{\text{det}} + \tau_{\text{act}} > t_{\text{harm}}\)), safety
  cannot rely on software. Physical containment must be delegated to
  passive hardware: series-elastic springs, pneumatic relief valves,
  torque-limiting slip clutches, and spring-applied fail-safe brakes.
\item
  \textbf{Accountable Human Signatures:} Operational risk cannot be
  dispersed across an anonymous team. Every release claim with an open
  residual gap must carry the explicit, legally accountable signature of
  named engineering leads who verify that the physical containment
  envelope renders the unknown harmless.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Systems Stress-Tests}\label{sec-frontier-17-9}

With the core epistemic limits, residual-claims register schemas,
detectorless failure mechanisms, and master architectural taxonomy
established, an engineer must be prepared to audit complex physical
systems at the boundary of empirical verification. The following four
systems stress-tests serve as capstone analytical exercises, challenging
you to diagnose observational indistinguishability, detectorless
physical aging, astronomical exposure traps, and latent manifold
shortcuts across embodied platforms:

\subsection*{Stress-Test 1: The Oily Surface Gradient (Observational
Indistinguishability)}\label{stress-test-1-the-oily-surface-gradient-observational-indistinguishability}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 1: The Oily Surface
Gradient (Observational Indistinguishability)}

\emph{The scenario.} An autonomous \(600\text{ kg}\) pallet-transport
robot navigates a smooth concrete warehouse concourse at
\(2.2\text{ m/s}\). An unmapped spill of transparent synthetic hydraulic
fluid (\(\mu = 0.10\)) covers a \(3\text{ m}\) patch of floor directly
ahead, presenting zero visual contrast to onboard RGB-D and LiDAR
sensors.

\emph{The systems dilemma.} Before the drive wheels enter the slick,
sensor telemetry is identical to clean dry concrete
(\(y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t)\)). By the time wheel encoders detect
differential angular slip, the kinematic stopping distance on
\(\mu = 0.10\) has expanded from \(0.45\text{ m}\) to \(2.51\text{ m}\),
breaching the \(0.80\text{ m}\) obstacle clearance buffer before the
vehicle can halt.

\emph{The systems verdict: Law of Physical Causality and
Irreversibility.} Safe stopping cannot be certified through vision-based
perception alone when the physical observable (friction coefficient
\(\mu\)) is unmeasurable prior to contact. The engineering authority
must derate maximum velocity to \(v \le 0.8\text{ m/s}\)
(\(E_{\text{kin}} \le 192\text{ J}\)) in mixed-traffic zones or install
forward polarimetric scatterometry, recording the unobservable surface
condition in the residual-claims register.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 2: Silent Thermal Demagnetization (Detectorless
Actuator
Aging)}\label{stress-test-2-silent-thermal-demagnetization-detectorless-actuator-aging}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 2: Silent Thermal
Demagnetization (Detectorless Actuator Aging)}

\emph{The scenario.} A 6-DoF robotic manipulator performs high-cadence
pick-and-place operations with heavy steel payloads. Over repeated duty
cycles, rotor eddy currents heat the NdFeB permanent magnets in Joint
3's motor past \(145^\circ\text{C}\), exceeding the magnet's thermal
ceiling and causing an irreversible \(30\%\) reduction in remanent
magnetic flux (\(B_r\)) and torque constant \(K_t\).

\emph{The systems dilemma.} Stator resistance temperature detectors
(RTDs) report nominal stator temperatures (\(75^\circ\text{C}\)), and
motor inverter current shunts report full commanded quadrature current
(\(I_q = 25\text{ A}\)). However, actual output electromagnetic torque
(\(\tau = K_t I_q\)) silently drops from \(50\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\) to
\(35\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\). When the arm transitions to cantilevered
gravity holding, the joint sags uncontrollably, striking a human
operator station in \(t_{\text{harm}} = 45\text{ ms}\).

\emph{The systems verdict: Law of Governed Change and Defensible
Release.} Stator-only thermal telemetry cannot detect rotor magnet flux
degradation at runtime. The machine must incorporate
high-Curie-temperature magnets (\(T_C > 310^\circ\text{C}\)),
spring-applied fail-safe friction brakes (de-energize to lock via
hardware interlock lines), and mandatory scheduled offline
torque-constant proof-tests on a dynamometer every 500 operating hours.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 3: The Astronomical Exposure Trap (Certifying
Open-World Edge
Cases)}\label{stress-test-3-the-astronomical-exposure-trap-certifying-open-world-edge-cases}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 3: The Astronomical
Exposure Trap (Certifying Open-World Edge Cases)}

\emph{The scenario.} An autonomous delivery vehicle developer logs 10
million accident-free operational miles (\(500{,}000\text{ hours}\))
across multiple urban deployments and submits a safety case claiming a
catastrophic collision probability \(p \le 10^{-8}/\text{hour}\) at
\(95\%\) statistical confidence for its end-to-end multimodal foundation
model.

\emph{The systems dilemma.} Under the zero-failure exposure bound
\(n \ge \frac{\ln(1/\alpha)}{p}\), certifying
\(p \le 10^{-8}/\text{hour}\) at \(95\%\) confidence (\(\alpha = 0.05\))
mathematically requires \(n \ge 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ hours}\) (over
34,200 machine-years) of independent, identically distributed exposure.
Furthermore, periodic over-the-air neural weight updates and correlated
weather patterns across the fleet continuously reset and invalidate
sample independence.

\emph{The systems verdict: Law of Information Freshness \& Zero-Failure
Exposure Bound.} Empirical black-box fleet testing is mathematically and
logically insufficient to certify ultra-rare tail safety in open
combinatorial environments. The release claim must be rejected unless
safety is guaranteed by an independent deterministic nervous-system
shield (CBF-QP enforcer running on an isolated MCU) holding exclusive
hardware veto authority over motor inverters.

\subsection*{Stress-Test 4: The Latent Manifold Shortcut (Specular Glare
in Brittle
Grasping)}\label{stress-test-4-the-latent-manifold-shortcut-specular-glare-in-brittle-grasping}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Stress-Test 4: The Latent Manifold
Shortcut (Specular Glare in Brittle Grasping)}

\emph{The scenario.} A high-precision dual-arm manipulator employs an
end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to insert thin glass
pharmaceutical ampoules into packaging trays. Direct late-afternoon
sunlight reflects off a stainless-steel workbench, casting caustic
specular glares across the camera sensor array.

\emph{The systems dilemma.} The high-dimensional visual encoder projects
the out-of-distribution optical flare onto the nominal latent manifold
(\(\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}_{\text{nom}}\)). The policy commands a
rapid downward plunging trajectory with near-zero softmax entropy
(\(H(\pi) \approx 0\)). Latent-space Mahalanobis distance uncertainty
estimators fail to flag the anomaly because the model is confident in
its corrupted representation. The gripper drives the glass ampoule into
the metal tray at \(300\text{ mm/s}\), shattering the vial in
\(14\text{ ms}\).

\emph{The systems verdict: Law of Proposal and Permission Privilege.}
High-capacity learned models cannot serve as their own safety
supervisors. Actuator commands must pass through a Proposal--Permission
boundary where a deterministic bare-metal nervous-system enforcer
monitors hardware load cells and laser proximity rangefinders at
\(1000\text{ Hz}\), backed by mechanical spring detents that decouple
force before glass fracture limits are reached.

The final frontier of physical AI is not algorithmic perfection, but
epistemic governance: establishing rigorous institutional and
architectural controls over what cannot be known. When an engineering
team acknowledges that open-world complexity, catastrophic tail risks,
and detectorless failure modes preclude absolute empirical certainty,
the safety argument does not collapse into paralysis. Instead, it
transitions from inductive confidence to deductive structural
containment. The governing instrument of this discipline is the
\textbf{Residual-Claims Register}---an immutable ledger that explicitly
records every unclosable claim, unmodeled physical parameter, and
unobservable state transition, pairing each with a permanent,
hardware-enforced containment boundary.

Where software cannot observe, hardware must constrain. If friction
coefficients on unmapped terrain cannot be guaranteed, velocity must be
physically clamped so that stopping distance remains within the shortest
possible line-of-sight clearance. If internal structural voids in
handled materials cannot be detected before contact, robotic
end-effectors must incorporate passive mechanical compliance---such as
spring-loaded flexures or torque-limiting slip clutches---that limit
peak impact forces below destructive thresholds regardless of software
commands. If neural network latent spaces cannot guarantee
out-of-distribution detection, the machine must operate behind physical
exclusion barriers or within certified geofenced corridors. Structural
containment renders epistemic uncertainty harmless by ensuring that when
the unknown occurs, the physical energy released remains strictly below
the threshold of catastrophic damage.

Ultimately, epistemic governance is a human accountability contract. An
autonomous system, no matter how sophisticated its neural architecture
or how extensive its training corpus, is a mathematical artifact lacking
legal personhood, moral agency, and the capacity to bear liability. When
a physical AI system damages property, disrupts critical infrastructure,
or harms a human being, responsibility cannot be diffused into the
opacity of high-dimensional latent spaces. The Cryptographic Release
Manifest established in Chapter~\ref{sec-release} binds the operational
authority of the machine directly to the cryptographic signatures of
designated systems engineers and adjudicators. Epistemic humility is
therefore not merely a philosophical virtue, but the core ethical and
professional discipline of physical AI systems engineering: recognizing
the limits of empirical proof, bounding physical authority through
deterministic hardware shields, and accepting personal accountability
for the machines we release into the physical world.

The synthesis of physical AI systems engineering is illustrated across
the three pillars in Figure~\ref{fig-17-closed-loop-synthesis}: the
\textbf{Brain} (which explores, plans, and optimizes across open-world
representations), the \textbf{Nervous System} (which arbitrates
authority, verifies intent leases, and enforces real-time barrier
certificates), and the \textbf{Body} (which interacts with continuum
mechanics under strict conservation laws).

\subsection*{Capstone Synthesis: The Three
Archetypes}\label{capstone-synthesis-the-three-archetypes}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Capstone Synthesis: The Three
Archetypes}

To close the curriculum, we revisit the Three Archetypes introduced in
earlier chapters, demonstrating how the complete physical AI framework
governs real hardware across diverse physical embodiments:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The Autonomous Mobile Manipulator (Mobile Archetype):}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \emph{Physical Substrate:} Differential-drive AGV with a 7-DOF
    articulated arm (\(m_{\text{total}} = 185\text{ kg}\),
    \(v_{\max} = 1.8\text{ m/s}\), payload \(10\text{ kg}\)).
  \item
    \emph{The Failure Mode:} Navigating a warehouse corridor under
    changing lighting, a vision-language policy misidentifies a thin,
    oil-slicked metal ramp as dry concrete, commanding a high-speed
    turning trajectory.
  \item
    \emph{The Systems Defense:} The exteroceptive Brain is blind to the
    low-friction hazard (observational indistinguishability). However,
    the deterministic Nervous System evaluates wheel slip ratios and IMU
    yaw rates at \(1000\text{ Hz}\). Detecting a micro-slip anomaly
    (\(s > 0.08\)) within \(4\text{ ms}\), the real-time MCU safety
    shield instantly overrides the policy's torque vectoring, clamps
    maximum velocity to \(0.4\text{ m/s}\) (firmware velocity derating),
    and engages \(\mathcal{C}^1\) bumpless deceleration along a
    straight-line stopping corridor.
  \item
    \emph{The Systems Verdict: Law of Structural Containment.} Safety
    did not depend on the VLA model recognizing oil; safety was
    guaranteed by the nervous system's deterministic traction barrier
    invariant.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{The High-Speed Collaborative Delta Robot (Manipulator
  Archetype):}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \emph{Physical Substrate:} 4-axis parallel kinematic delta robot
    (\(v_{\text{tool}} \le 4.0\text{ m/s}\), cycle rate
    \(120\text{ picks/min}\)) sorting food products alongside human
    packing personnel.
  \item
    \emph{The Failure Mode:} A worker reaches into the shared pick zone
    to clear a jammed carton. The robot's learned object-tracking head
    experiences a transient \(45\text{ ms}\) GPU kernel scheduling
    stall, causing an intent lease timeout.
  \item
    \emph{The Systems Defense:} The nervous system's windowed hardware
    watchdog detects heartbeat absence within \(3.0\text{ ms}\). The
    Simplex switch trips, immediately transferring motor authority from
    the stalled Linux MPU to a precomputed quintic deceleration spline
    resident in microcontroller SRAM TCM. Actuators smoothly arrest
    motion within \(18\text{ ms}\) (\(d_{\text{stop}} = 36\text{ mm}\)),
    strictly respecting ISO/TS 15066 transient impact force limits
    (\(F \le 50\text{ N}\)).
  \item
    \emph{The Systems Verdict: Law of Asymmetric Authority.} The
    high-level neural policy proposes; the bare-metal safety enforcer
    permits. When deliberation stalls, the nervous system enforces
    zero-command containment without waiting for software recovery.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  \textbf{The Continuous Chemical Reaction Furnace (Process Archetype):}

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    \emph{Physical Substrate:} Exothermic batch reactor with
    variable-speed reactant injection pumps and proportional cooling
    jacket valves (\(P_{\max} = 4.5\text{ MPa}\),
    \(T_{\max} = 450^\circ\text{C}\)).
  \item
    \emph{The Failure Mode:} An adaptive neural optimization policy
    adjusts reactant feed rates to maximize yield. A sudden supply batch
    variance introduces an unmodeled catalytic promoter, initiating
    thermal runaway with temperature rising at
    \(\dot{T} = 12.5^\circ\text{C/s}\).
  \item
    \emph{The Systems Defense:} The neural optimizer misinterprets the
    rapid temperature rise as a productive yield surge. However, an
    independent Control Barrier Function running on an isolated lockstep
    safety controller continuously evaluates the thermal-hydraulic
    barrier \(h(T, P) = T_{\max} - T - \tau_{\text{cool}}\dot{T}\). The
    moment \(h(T, P) \le 0\), the enforcer asserts hardwired Safe Torque
    Off (STO) to the feed pumps and commands 100\% duty cycle to the
    emergency quench coolant valve via direct memory-mapped PWM
    registers, bypassing the Linux optimizer entirely.
  \item
    \emph{The Systems Verdict: Law of Proposal and Permission
    Privilege.} High-capacity learned models cannot serve as their own
    safety supervisors. Actuator commands must pass through a
    Proposal--Permission boundary where a deterministic bare-metal
    nervous-system enforcer monitors hardware load cells and laser
    proximity rangefinders at \(1000\text{ Hz}\), backed by mechanical
    spring detents that decouple force before glass fracture limits are
    reached.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\section{Summary}\label{sec-frontier-17-10}

The central question posed at the opening of this book---\emph{why does
an error that costs nothing on a screen destroy hardware in the physical
world?}---finds its ultimate resolution at this frontier. Software
operating behind glass enjoys the luxury of idempotency. An embodied
machine operating in the physical world is bound by conservation laws:
delay is paid in physical displacement (\(d = v \tau\)), kinetic energy
cannot be recalled once released, and unmonitored physical invariants
drift regardless of model confidence. The frontier of physical AI is
therefore not a catalog of speculative algorithms, but the permanent
boundary where measurable evidence ends and structural containment
begins. A machine is safe to operate not when its learned models appear
competent, but when its nervous system ensures that failure remains
physically bounded.

\phantomsection\label{callout-takeaways*-17.7}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The Epistemic Boundary is Permanent (Residual-Claims
  Register):} Empirical verification can never test the full
  combinatorial open world. Every physical AI release requires an
  explicit Residual-Claims Register that identifies unclosable
  hypotheses and binds each to a deterministic physical or mechanical
  containment mechanism.
\item
  \textbf{Observational Indistinguishability Demands Structural
  Containment:} When safe and catastrophic physical states emit
  identical pre-harm sensor signals (\(y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t)\)) until the
  reaction window is exhausted
  (\(\tau_{\text{det}} + \tau_{\text{act}} > t_{\text{harm}}\)),
  software cannot prevent damage. Safety must be enforced through
  passive mechanical compliance, slip clutches, or velocity derating.
\item
  \textbf{The Astronomical Exposure Wall Precludes Black-Box Statistical
  Proofs:} Validating an ultra-reliable safety claim
  (\(p \le 10^{-8}/\text{hour}\)) requires
  \(>3.0 \times 10^8\text{ hours}\) (34,200 machine-years) of
  failure-free exposure---a mathematical impossibility. High-assurance
  physical safety rests exclusively on architectural isolation and
  deterministic runtime enforcers.
\item
  \textbf{The Proposal--Permission Architectural Invariant:} Across all
  embodiments (mobile robots, manipulators, continuous chemical plants),
  high-capacity neural foundation models propose actions (\(p_t\)),
  while bare-metal real-time microcontrollers hold exclusive hardware
  veto authority over power inverters (\(1000\text{ Hz}\)).
\item
  \textbf{The Sovereign Master Law of Physical AI:} Software behind
  glass enjoys idempotency; in the physical universe, computational
  delay is paid in millimeters (\(\Delta x = \int v \, dt\)), kinetic
  energy cannot be recalled, and safety is achieved only when failure
  remains physically bounded.
\end{itemize}

For systems, embedded, and software engineers, mathematical formulas in

\section*{1. Kinematics and Stopping
Envelopes}\label{kinematics-and-stopping-envelopes}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{1. Kinematics and Stopping Envelopes}

\markright{1. Kinematics and Stopping Envelopes}

\subsection*{The Physical Derivation of Stopping
Distance}\label{the-physical-derivation-of-stopping-distance}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{The Physical Derivation of Stopping
Distance}

\lettrine{W}{hen} an embodied robot maneuvers at linear velocity
\(v(t)\), the distance required to bring its physical mass to a
complete, controlled stop consists of two decoupled components:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Reaction Drift (\(d_{\text{drift}}\)):} The distance traversed
  while sensory signals propagate through transduction, bus
  serialization, neural inference, and communication queues before the
  actuators can apply braking torque.
\item
  \textbf{Kinematic Braking (\(d_{\text{brake}}\)):} The distance
  traversed while physical friction or counter-electromotive braking
  forces decelerate the moving mass at maximum safe deceleration
  \(a_{\text{max}}\).
\end{enumerate}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}@{}}

\textbf{Phase 1: Reaction Drift} & Sensor exposure, neural inference,
network transport, inverter rise &
\(d_{\text{drift}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}}\) &
\(t \in [0, \tau_{\text{latency}}]\) \\
\textbf{Phase 2: Kinematic Braking} & Counter-EMF braking, friction,
ground adhesion & \(d_{\text{brake}} = \dfrac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}\) &
\(t \in [\tau_{\text{latency}}, t_{\text{stop}}]\) \\
\end{longtable}

Integrating Newtonian dynamics under constant deceleration
\(a(t) = -a_{\text{max}}\):

\[v(t) = v_0 - a_{\text{max}} t \implies t_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v_0}{a_{\text{max}}}\]

\[d_{\text{brake}} = \int_0^{t_{\text{brake}}} (v_0 - a_{\text{max}} t) \, dt = v_0 t_{\text{brake}} - \frac{1}{2} a_{\text{max}} t_{\text{brake}}^2 = \frac{v_0^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}\]

Accounting for total sensorimotor transport latency
\(\tau_{\text{latency}}\), the \textbf{Total Dynamic Stopping Envelope}
is:

\[d_{\text{stop}}(v) = \underbrace{v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}}}_{\text{Reaction Drift}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}}_{\text{Kinematic Braking}}\]

where: * \(v\): Current operational velocity (\(\text{m/s}\)). *
\(\tau_{\text{latency}}\): Total end-to-end transport delay
(\(\text{s}\)), encompassing camera exposure, bus serialization
(CAN-FD/PCIe), operating system scheduling tail latency, and inverter
current rise time. * \(a_{\text{max}}\): Maximum permissible physical
braking deceleration (\(\text{m/s}^2\)), constrained by tire friction
coefficient (\(\mu g\)), payload tipping limits, or motor peak torque.

\subsection*{Parabolic Safe Velocity
Clamping}\label{parabolic-safe-velocity-clamping}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Parabolic Safe Velocity Clamping}

Given a measured physical clearance \(d_{\text{clearance}}\) to an
obstacle and a safety margin \(d_{\text{margin}}\), the maximum safe
operational velocity \(v_{\text{safe}}\) is derived by solving the
quadratic inequality
\(d_{\text{stop}}(v) \le d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{margin}}\):

\[\frac{1}{2 a_{\text{max}}} v^2 + \tau_{\text{latency}} v - (d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{margin}}) \le 0\]

Applying the quadratic formula and selecting the positive root:

\[v_{\text{safe}} = \sqrt{a_{\text{max}}^2 \tau_{\text{latency}}^2 + 2 a_{\text{max}} (d_{\text{clearance}} - d_{\text{margin}})} - a_{\text{max}} \tau_{\text{latency}}\]

\subsection*{Microcontroller Execution Complexity and Timing
Bounds}\label{microcontroller-execution-complexity-and-timing-bounds}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Microcontroller Execution Complexity
and Timing Bounds}

In real-time firmware, evaluating \(v_{\text{safe}}\) and
\(d_{\text{stop}}(v)\) executes at \(1000\text{ Hz}\) in static SRAM
with zero dynamic memory allocation (\texttt{malloc\ =\ 0}). Because the
formulation requires only a single square-root operation and basic
floating-point arithmetic, its Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) on a
\(480\text{ MHz}\) ARM Cortex-M7 with a hardware Floating Point Unit
(FPU) is bounded to \(\text{WCET} \le 1.2\,\mu\text{s}\), consuming less
than \(0.15\%\) of the \(1.0\text{ ms}\) control interval.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section*{2. Spatial Geometry and Lie
Algebra}\label{spatial-geometry-and-lie-algebra}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{2. Spatial Geometry and Lie Algebra}

\markright{2. Spatial Geometry and Lie Algebra}

Physical AI agents operate in three-dimensional Euclidean space
\(\mathbb{R}^3\). To transform sensor observations, object affordances,
and robot kinematics across coordinate frames, systems rely on the
Special Euclidean Group \(SE(3)\).

\subsection*{Homogeneous Transformation
Matrices}\label{homogeneous-transformation-matrices}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Homogeneous Transformation Matrices}

A rigid-body transformation from coordinate frame \(A\) to coordinate
frame \(B\) consists of a 3D rotation \(\mathbf{R}_A^B \in SO(3)\) and a
3D translation \(\mathbf{p}_A^B \in \mathbb{R}^3\), unified into a
\(4 \times 4\) homogeneous matrix \(\mathbf{T}_A^B \in SE(3)\):

\[\mathbf{T}_A^B = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_A^B & \mathbf{p}_A^B \\ \mathbf{0}_{1 \times 3} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}\]

Points in 3D space are transformed using homogeneous coordinates
\(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = [\mathbf{x}^T, 1]^T\):

\[\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_B = \mathbf{T}_A^B \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_A \implies \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_B \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}_A^B \mathbf{x}_A + \mathbf{p}_A^B \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Matrix inversion in \(SE(3)\) has a closed-form structure that avoids
general \(4 \times 4\) Gaussian elimination:

\[(\mathbf{T}_A^B)^{-1} = \mathbf{T}_B^A = \begin{bmatrix} (\mathbf{R}_A^B)^T & -(\mathbf{R}_A^B)^T \mathbf{p}_A^B \\ \mathbf{0}_{1 \times 3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

\subsection*{Quaternions for Singularity-Free
Rotations}\label{quaternions-for-singularity-free-rotations}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Quaternions for Singularity-Free
Rotations}

While Euler angles (Roll, Pitch, Yaw) suffer from kinematic
singularities (\textbf{Gimbal Lock} when pitch approaches
\(\pm 90^\circ\), causing division by zero in coordinate
transformations), unit quaternions provide a continuous, computationally
robust 4-parameter representation:

\[\mathbf{q} = [w, x, y, z]^T = [\cos(\theta / 2), \mathbf{u}^T \sin(\theta / 2)]^T, \quad \|\mathbf{q}\|_2^2 = w^2 + x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\]

where \(\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) is the unit rotation axis and
\(\theta\) is the rotation angle.

The \textbf{Hamilton Quaternion Product}
(\(\mathbf{q}_c = \mathbf{q}_a \otimes \mathbf{q}_b\)) compounds
successive 3D rotations:

\[\mathbf{q}_a \otimes \mathbf{q}_b = \begin{bmatrix}
w_a w_b - x_a x_b - y_a y_b - z_a z_b \\
w_a x_b + x_a w_b + y_a z_b - z_a y_b \\
w_a y_b - x_a z_b + y_a w_b + z_a x_b \\
w_a z_b + x_a y_b - y_a x_b + z_a w_b
\end{bmatrix}\]

\subsection*{Lie Algebra and Tangent Space
Integration}\label{lie-algebra-and-tangent-space-integration}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Lie Algebra and Tangent Space
Integration}

In high-frequency control loops (\(1000\text{ Hz}\)), velocities are
expressed as continuous \textbf{spatial twists}
\(\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^6\) combining linear velocity
\(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) and angular velocity
\(\boldsymbol{\omega} \in \mathbb{R}^3\):

\[\boldsymbol{\xi} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ \boldsymbol{\omega} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^6\]

The wedge operator \((\cdot)^\wedge\) maps
\(\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^6\) to the matrix Lie algebra
\(\mathfrak{se}(3)\):

\[\boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge = \begin{bmatrix} [\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times & \mathbf{v} \\ \mathbf{0}_{1 \times 3} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}, \quad \text{where } [\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega_z & \omega_y \\ \omega_z & 0 & -\omega_x \\ -\omega_y & \omega_x & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Integrating a constant twist \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) over a discrete time
step \(\Delta t\) updates the robot pose without numerical distortion
using the \textbf{Exponential Map}:

\[\mathbf{T}(t + \Delta t) = \mathbf{T}(t) \cdot \exp\left( \boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge \Delta t \right)\]

\[\exp\left( \boldsymbol{\xi}^\wedge \Delta t \right) = \begin{bmatrix} \exp([\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times \Delta t) & \mathbf{V}\mathbf{v}\Delta t \\ \mathbf{0}_{1 \times 3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

where the left-Jacobian matrix \(\mathbf{V}\) and rotation matrix
\(\exp([\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times \Delta t)\) are evaluated in closed
form via Rodrigues' formula with
\(\theta = \|\boldsymbol{\omega}\| \Delta t\):

\[\exp([\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times \Delta t) = \mathbf{I}_{3 \times 3} + \frac{\sin(\theta)}{\theta}[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times + \frac{1 - \cos(\theta)}{\theta^2}[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times^2\]

\[\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_{3 \times 3} + \frac{1 - \cos(\theta)}{\theta^2}[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times + \frac{\theta - \sin(\theta)}{\theta^3}[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times^2\]

\subsection*{Numerical Normalization
Invariant}\label{numerical-normalization-invariant}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Numerical Normalization Invariant}

Under discrete integration, floating-point round-off causes unit
quaternions to drift (\(\|\mathbf{q}\| \neq 1\)), corrupting the
\(SO(3)\) rotation manifold. In real-time \(1000\text{ Hz}\) state
estimators, the quaternion is renormalized every cycle
(\(\mathbf{q} \gets \mathbf{q} / \|\mathbf{q}\|\)), falling back to
identity \([1, 0, 0, 0]^T\) if \(\|\mathbf{q}\|^2 < 10^{-12}\),
executing in \(< 0.1\,\mu\text{s}\) with zero dynamic memory allocation.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section*{3. Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic
Programs}\label{control-barrier-functions-and-quadratic-programs}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{3. Control Barrier Functions and
Quadratic Programs}

\markright{3. Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programs}

\subsection*{Forward Invariance and Nagumo's
Theorem}\label{forward-invariance-and-nagumos-theorem}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Forward Invariance and Nagumo's
Theorem}

Consider a control-affine physical dynamical system:

\[\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}\]

where \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the physical state (positions,
velocities), \(\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) is the control input (motor
torques, phase voltages), and \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\) and
\(g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}\) describe the autonomous
drift dynamics and control input mapping. Both \(f\) and \(g\) are
assumed to be locally Lipschitz continuous.

A physical safe operating set \(\mathcal{C} \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is
defined as the 0-superlevel set of a continuously differentiable scalar
barrier certificate function
\(h(\mathbf{x}): \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\):

\[\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \}\]

\[\partial \mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid h(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \} \quad (\text{Safety Boundary})\]

\[\text{Int}(\mathcal{C}) = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid h(\mathbf{x}) > 0 \} \quad (\text{Safe Interior})\]

The safe set \(\mathcal{C}\) is \textbf{forward invariant} if for every
initial physical state starting within the set
(\(\mathbf{x}(0) \in \mathcal{C}\)), the trajectory remains safe for all
future time: \(\mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathcal{C}, \forall t \ge 0\).

\subsubsection*{Formal Proof of Forward Invariance via Nagumo's
Condition}\label{formal-proof-of-forward-invariance-via-nagumos-condition}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{Formal Proof of Forward Invariance
via Nagumo's Condition}

Nagumo's theorem for set invariance states that a closed set
\(\mathcal{C}\) is forward invariant under the vector field
\(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = F(\mathbf{x})\) if and only if the velocity vector
\(F(\mathbf{x})\) points into the tangent cone (subtangent vectors) of
\(\mathcal{C}\) at every boundary point
\(\mathbf{x} \in \partial \mathcal{C}\):

\[\forall \mathbf{x} \in \partial \mathcal{C}, \quad \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot F(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0\]

To guarantee asymptotic stability of the safe set and avoid edge
chatter, we enforce the generalized Control Barrier Function condition
with an extended class-\(\mathcal{K}\) function \(\alpha(\cdot)\) (where
\(\alpha(0) = 0\) and \(\alpha\) is strictly increasing):

\[\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) [f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}] \ge -\alpha(h(\mathbf{x}))\]

Choosing the canonical linear class-\(\mathcal{K}\) form
\(\alpha(h) = \gamma h\) with rate parameter \(\gamma > 0\), the
differential inequality becomes:

\[\frac{d h(\mathbf{x}(t))}{dt} \ge -\gamma h(\mathbf{x}(t))\]

Applying the Comparison Lemma (Grönwall's Inequality) to this scalar
differential inequality yields:

\[h(\mathbf{x}(t)) \ge h(\mathbf{x}(0)) e^{-\gamma t}, \quad \forall t \ge 0\]

Because \(h(\mathbf{x}(0)) \ge 0\) for any state starting in
\(\mathcal{C}\) and the exponential decay term \(e^{-\gamma t} > 0\) for
all finite \(t \in [0, \infty)\), it follows that:

\[h(\mathbf{x}(t)) \ge 0, \quad \forall t \ge 0\]

Thus, the state trajectory \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) can never cross the zero
boundary \(\partial \mathcal{C}\), proving rigorous mathematical forward
set invariance.

\subsection*{Lie Derivatives and Affine Control
Invariants}\label{lie-derivatives-and-affine-control-invariants}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Lie Derivatives and Affine Control
Invariants}

Expanding \(\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})\) via the chain rule:

\[\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) [f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}] = \underbrace{\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) f(\mathbf{x})}_{L_f h(\mathbf{x})} + \underbrace{\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) g(\mathbf{x})}_{L_g h(\mathbf{x})} \mathbf{u}\]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{\(L_f h(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}\):} The \emph{Lie
  derivative along \(f\)}, representing the natural physical rate of
  change of safety clearance under zero actuator power (unforced
  momentum drift).
\item
  \textbf{\(L_g h(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times m}\):} The
  \emph{Lie derivative along \(g\)}, representing the control authority
  over safety clearance per unit actuator input.
\end{itemize}

The Control Barrier Function condition becomes an \textbf{affine linear
inequality} in the control input vector \(\mathbf{u}\):

\[L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \gamma h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0\]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{The Speed Governor Invariant:} When far inside the safe set
  (\(h(\mathbf{x}) \gg 0\)), \(-\gamma h(\mathbf{x})\) evaluates to a
  large negative number, leaving the candidate control input
  \(\mathbf{u}\) unconstrained. As physical clearance collapses toward
  the boundary (\(h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0\)),
  \(-\gamma h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0\), forcing the approach speed
  \(\dot{h} \ge 0\). At the exact boundary (\(h=0\)), any action that
  produces negative clearance rate is strictly vetoed, rendering the
  boundary mathematically impenetrable.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Program
(CBF-QP)}\label{the-minimal-intervention-quadratic-program-cbf-qp}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{The Minimal-Intervention Quadratic
Program (CBF-QP)}

In the Proposal--Permission architecture, upstream neural policies
(System 2 / System 1.5) emit unverified candidate action proposals
\(\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \in \mathbb{R}^m\). The bare-metal
microcontroller (System 1) solves the following convex Quadratic Program
at \(1000\text{ Hz}\):

\[\mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m} \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}})^T \mathbf{W} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}})\]

\[\begin{aligned}
\text{subject to:} \quad &L_f h_i(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \gamma_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0, \quad i = 1, \dots, M \\
&\mathbf{u}_{\text{min}} \le \mathbf{u} \le \mathbf{u}_{\text{max}}
\end{aligned}\]

where \(\mathbf{W} \succ 0\) is a positive-definite weighting metric.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Minimal Intervention Principle:} When
  \(\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}\) satisfies all barrier inequalities, the
  objective is minimized at \(\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}\)
  with zero active constraints, passing the AI policy's action
  unmodified. When \(\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}\) violates a barrier, the
  QP executes an orthogonal projection onto the safe half-space boundary
  \(\partial \mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}\), modifying the command by the
  minimum Euclidean perturbation required to preserve invariance.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Multi-Variable KKT Matrix System and Active-Set
Derivation}\label{multi-variable-kkt-matrix-system-and-active-set-derivation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Multi-Variable KKT Matrix System and
Active-Set Derivation}

Writing the CBF-QP in standard matrix inequality form:

\[\min_{\mathbf{u}} \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{u} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbf{A} \mathbf{u} \ge \mathbf{b}\]

where the constraint matrix \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times m}\)
and vector \(\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^K\) stack both the \(M\) barrier
constraints and the \(2m\) box limits (\(K = M + 2m\)):

\[\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} L_g h_1(\mathbf{x}) \\ \vdots \\ L_g h_M(\mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{I}_{m \times m} \\ -\mathbf{I}_{m \times m} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} -L_f h_1(\mathbf{x}) - \gamma_1 h_1(\mathbf{x}) \\ \vdots \\ -L_f h_M(\mathbf{x}) - \gamma_M h_M(\mathbf{x}) \\ \mathbf{u}_{\text{min}} \\ -\mathbf{u}_{\text{max}} \end{bmatrix}\]

The Lagrangian function for this convex optimization problem is:

\[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{u}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}})^T \mathbf{W} (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}) - \boldsymbol{\lambda}^T (\mathbf{A} \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{b})\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^K\) is the vector of
non-negative Lagrange multipliers. The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT)
optimality conditions are:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Stationarity:}
  \(\nabla_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{W} (\mathbf{u}^* - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}) - \mathbf{A}^T \boldsymbol{\lambda}^* = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} + \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}^T \boldsymbol{\lambda}^*\)
\item
  \textbf{Primal Feasibility:}
  \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{u}^* - \mathbf{b} \ge \mathbf{0}\)
\item
  \textbf{Dual Feasibility:} \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^* \ge \mathbf{0}\)
\item
  \textbf{Complementary Slackness:}
  \(\lambda_k^* (\mathbf{a}_k^T \mathbf{u}^* - b_k) = 0, \quad \forall k \in \{1, \dots, K\}\)
\end{enumerate}

Let \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \{1, \dots, K\}\) denote the active
constraint set at the optimal solution (where
\(\mathbf{a}_k^T \mathbf{u}^* = b_k\) and \(\lambda_k^* > 0\)).
Restricting \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) to the active rows
\(\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}\):

\[\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \left( \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} + \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^* \right) = \mathbf{b}_{\mathcal{A}}\]

Rearranging yields the symmetric positive-definite active-set linear
system for the optimal dual variables:

\[\left( \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T \right) \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^* = \mathbf{b}_{\mathcal{A}} - \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}\]

Solving for \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^*\) via Cholesky
decomposition
\(\mathbf{L} \mathbf{L}^T = \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T\),
the optimal projected control command is:

\[\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} + \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T \boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\mathcal{A}}^*\]

\subsection*{Microcontroller Real-Time Solvers and Complexity
Bounds}\label{microcontroller-real-time-solvers-and-complexity-bounds}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Microcontroller Real-Time Solvers and
Complexity Bounds}

On safety-critical microcontrollers (such as a dual-core lockstep ARM
Cortex-M7 at \(480\text{ MHz}\)), solving the active-set CBF-QP is
executed using static memory allocations in Data Tightly-Coupled Memory
(DTCM) with zero heap fragmentation (\texttt{malloc\ =\ 0}).

For a 6-DoF manipulator with \(M=8\) active barrier certificates, the
active-set algorithm resolves the optimal projection in \(3\text{--}6\)
iterations. Each iteration performs a Cholesky factorization of the
small active-set Gram matrix
\((\mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}} \mathbf{W}^{-1} \mathbf{A}_{\mathcal{A}}^T) \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}| \times |\mathcal{A}|}\)
(where \(|\mathcal{A}| \le 6\)). On target silicon, nominal solve time
is under \(45\,\mu\text{s}\), with a hard worst-case execution time
bounded to \(\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}\) at maximum iteration
count (\(k_{\text{max}} = 10\)). If the active-set fails to converge
within \(10\) iterations, the microcontroller deterministically aborts
to the Category 1 dynamic stopping trajectory (\(a = -a_{\text{max}}\))
within the remaining \(825\,\mu\text{s}\) of the \(1.0\text{ ms}\)
control cycle.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section*{4. Continuous-Discrete Extended Kalman
Filtering}\label{continuous-discrete-extended-kalman-filtering}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{4. Continuous-Discrete Extended Kalman
Filtering}

\markright{4. Continuous-Discrete Extended Kalman Filtering}

Physical AI pipelines fuse high-rate (\(1000\text{ Hz}\)) noisy
proprioceptive inertial measurements with delayed, multi-modal
exteroceptive observations (\(10\text{--}30\text{ Hz}\)) using the
\textbf{Continuous-Discrete Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)}.

\subsection*{Continuous Physics Error Dynamics and Riccati ODE
Derivation}\label{continuous-physics-error-dynamics-and-riccati-ode-derivation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Continuous Physics Error Dynamics and
Riccati ODE Derivation}

Between discrete measurement arrivals, the continuous physical state
evolves under non-linear dynamics with continuous process noise:

\[\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = f(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{u}(t)) + \mathbf{w}(t), \qquad \mathbf{w}(t) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_c(t))\]

The estimated state mean propagates via the nominal dynamics:

\[\dot{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(t) = f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t), \mathbf{u}(t))\]

Defining estimation error
\(\mathbf{e}(t) = \mathbf{x}(t) - \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t)\) and linearizing
\(f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})\) via Taylor expansion about
\(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t)\):

\[f(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{u}(t)) = f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t), \mathbf{u}(t)) + \mathbf{F}(t)\mathbf{e}(t) + \mathcal{O}(\|\mathbf{e}\|^2), \qquad \mathbf{F}(t) = \left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}(t), \mathbf{u}(t)}\]

The continuous error dynamics satisfy:

\[\dot{\mathbf{e}}(t) = \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) - \dot{\hat{\mathbf{x}}}(t) = \mathbf{F}(t)\mathbf{e}(t) + \mathbf{w}(t)\]

The spatial error covariance matrix is defined as the expectation
\(\mathbf{P}(t) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}(t)\mathbf{e}(t)^T]\). Applying
the product rule for differentiation:

\[\dot{\mathbf{P}}(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}(t)\mathbf{e}(t)^T] = \mathbb{E}[\dot{\mathbf{e}}(t)\mathbf{e}(t)^T] + \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}(t)\dot{\mathbf{e}}(t)^T]\]

Substituting the error differential equation:

\[\mathbb{E}[\dot{\mathbf{e}}(t)\mathbf{e}(t)^T] = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{F}(t)\mathbf{e}(t) + \mathbf{w}(t))\mathbf{e}(t)^T] = \mathbf{F}(t)\mathbf{P}(t) + \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{w}(t)\mathbf{e}(t)^T]\]

Because white Gaussian process noise \(\mathbf{w}(t)\) is uncorrelated
with past estimation errors,
\(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{w}(t)\mathbf{e}(t)^T] = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{Q}_c(t)\).
Adding the transpose term yields the \textbf{Continuous Matrix Riccati
Differential Equation}:

\[\dot{\mathbf{P}}(t) = \mathbf{F}(t)\mathbf{P}(t) + \mathbf{P}(t)\mathbf{F}(t)^T + \mathbf{Q}_c(t)\]

Discretizing across integration time step \(\Delta t = 1.0\text{ ms}\):

\[\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1} + \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}(\tau), \mathbf{u}_{k-1})\,d\tau \approx \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1} + f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1|k-1}, \mathbf{u}_{k-1})\Delta t\]

\[\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}_k \mathbf{P}_{k-1|k-1} \boldsymbol{\Phi}_k^T + \mathbf{Q}_d\]

where
\(\boldsymbol{\Phi}_k \approx \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{F}(t_{k-1})\Delta t\)
is the state transition matrix and
\(\mathbf{Q}_d \approx \mathbf{Q}_c \Delta t\) is discrete process noise
covariance.

\subsection*{Optimal Kalman Gain Derivation via Minimum Trace
Estimation}\label{optimal-kalman-gain-derivation-via-minimum-trace-estimation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Optimal Kalman Gain Derivation via
Minimum Trace Estimation}

When a discrete measurement \(\mathbf{z}_k \in \mathbb{R}^m\) arrives at
time \(t_k\):

\[\mathbf{z}_k = h(\mathbf{x}_k) + \mathbf{v}_k, \qquad \mathbf{v}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_k)\]

The linear estimator updates the state estimate according to:

\[\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1} + \mathbf{K}_k (\mathbf{z}_k - h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}))\]

Linearizing the observation function
\(h(\mathbf{x}_k) \approx h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}) + \mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{e}_{k|k-1}\)
with
\(\mathbf{H}_k = \left. \frac{\partial h}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1}}\),
the a posteriori error is:

\[\mathbf{e}_{k|k} = \mathbf{x}_k - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{e}_{k|k-1} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{v}_k\]

Evaluating the a posteriori covariance
\(\mathbf{P}_{k|k} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{e}_{k|k}\mathbf{e}_{k|k}^T]\)
under mutually independent state error and sensor noise:

\[\mathbf{P}_{k|k} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)^T + \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{K}_k^T\]

To find the gain \(\mathbf{K}_k\) minimizing the mean squared estimation
error, we minimize the scalar cost function
\(J = \text{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{k|k})\). Expanding the trace:

\[J = \text{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}) - 2\text{Tr}(\mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1}) + \text{Tr}\left(\mathbf{K}_k (\mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k)\mathbf{K}_k^T\right)\]

Applying matrix differentiation identities
\(\frac{\partial \text{Tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})}{\partial \mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{B}^T\)
and
\(\frac{\partial \text{Tr}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{A}^T)}{\partial \mathbf{A}} = 2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{C}\)
(for symmetric \(\mathbf{C}\)):

\[\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mathbf{K}_k} = -2 (\mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1})^T + 2 \mathbf{K}_k (\mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k) = \mathbf{0}\]

Defining innovation covariance
\(\mathbf{S}_k = \mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k\):

\[\mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{S}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \implies \mathbf{K}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{S}_k^{-1}\]

\subsection*{Structural Proof of the Joseph Stabilized Covariance
Form}\label{structural-proof-of-the-joseph-stabilized-covariance-form}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Structural Proof of the Joseph
Stabilized Covariance Form}

On 32-bit embedded architectures (FP32), the simplified covariance
update \(\mathbf{P} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{P}\)
causes catastrophic divergence due to numerical asymmetry and lost
positive definiteness.

The \textbf{Joseph stabilized form} guarantees positive
semi-definiteness:

\[\mathbf{P}_{k|k} = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k) \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)^T + \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{K}_k^T\]

\textbf{Mathematical Proof of Global Stability:} Let
\(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) be an arbitrary non-zero test vector.
The quadratic form evaluates to:

\[\mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{P}_{k|k} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}^T (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k) \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)^T \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{K}_k^T \mathbf{y}\]

Defining transformed vectors
\(\mathbf{u}_1 = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)^T \mathbf{y}\)
and \(\mathbf{u}_2 = \mathbf{K}_k^T \mathbf{y}\):

\[\mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{P}_{k|k} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{u}_1^T \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{u}_2^T \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{u}_2\]

Because \(\mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \succeq 0\) and \(\mathbf{R}_k \succ 0\):

\[\mathbf{u}_1^T \mathbf{P}_{k|k-1} \mathbf{u}_1 \ge 0, \qquad \mathbf{u}_2^T \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{u}_2 \ge 0 \implies \mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{P}_{k|k} \mathbf{y} \ge 0 \quad \forall \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\]

Thus, \(\mathbf{P}_{k|k}\) is strictly positive semi-definite
(\(\mathbf{P}_{k|k} \succeq 0\)) regardless of floating-point truncation
errors or suboptimal gain matrices.

\subsection*{Mahalanobis Innovation
Gating}\label{mahalanobis-innovation-gating}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Mahalanobis Innovation Gating}

The measurement innovation
\(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k = \mathbf{z}_k - h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k|k-1})\)
represents the new information introduced by the sensor. Under Gaussian
assumptions,
\(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{S}_k)\).

The squared Mahalanobis distance scales the innovation residual by its
expected uncertainty:

\[d_M^2 = \tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k^T \mathbf{S}_k^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{y}}_k \sim \chi_m^2\]

where \(m = \dim(\mathbf{z}_k)\). The gating threshold is evaluated
against the cumulative Chi-Square distribution:

\[\text{Decision} = \begin{cases} \text{Accept Measurement and Apply Update}, & d_M^2 \le \chi_{m, 1-\alpha}^2 \\\\ \text{Reject Outlier and Propagate Open-Loop}, & d_M^2 > \chi_{m, 1-\alpha}^2 \end{cases}\]

\subsection*{Real-Time Kalman Filter Determinism and
Complexity}\label{real-time-kalman-filter-determinism-and-complexity}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Real-Time Kalman Filter Determinism
and Complexity}

In embedded state estimation pipelines, the Continuous-Discrete EKF
executes on dedicated microcontroller hardware or real-time DSPs in
static DTCM SRAM with zero dynamic memory allocation
(\texttt{malloc\ =\ 0}).

For a 6-dimensional kinematic state (\(n=6\)) with 3-dimensional
position observations (\(m=3\)), the propagation step requires
\(O(n^3)\) operations (\(216\) multiply-accumulates), and the
Joseph-form measurement update requires matrix inversion of the
\(3 \times 3\) innovation covariance \(\mathbf{S}_k\), followed by outer
product updates
\(\mathbf{P}_k = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_k^-(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)^T + \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{R}_k\mathbf{K}_k^T\).

On an ARM Cortex-M7 with hardware SIMD and single-precision FPU, the
complete propagation and Joseph update cycle executes in under
\(18.5\,\mu\text{s}\) (\(\text{WCET} \le 25.0\,\mu\text{s}\)), ensuring
that state estimates and uncertainty bounds are updated with
deterministic microsecond precision before feeding downstream Control
Barrier Functions.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section*{5. Field-Oriented Motor
Control}\label{field-oriented-motor-control}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{5. Field-Oriented Motor Control}

\markright{5. Field-Oriented Motor Control}

To translate high-level torque commands into physical electromagnetic
forces, brushless permanent-magnet synchronous motors (PMSM) rely on
\textbf{Field-Oriented Control (FOC)} executing in dedicated hardware
timer peripherals at \(20\text{ kHz}\) (\(\Delta t = 50\,\mu\text{s}\)).

\subsection*{Clarke Transformation}\label{clarke-transformation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Clarke Transformation}

Transforms balanced three-phase stator currents \((i_a, i_b, i_c)\) into
a stationary two-phase orthogonal coordinate system:

\[\begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix} = \frac{2}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_a \\ i_b \\ i_c \end{bmatrix}\]

Using the zero-sum property \(i_a + i_b + i_c = 0\), this simplifies to:

\[i_\alpha = i_a, \quad i_\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} (i_a + 2 i_b)\]

\subsection*{Park Transformation}\label{park-transformation}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Park Transformation}

Rotates the stationary \((\alpha, \beta)\) currents into the rotor's
rotating reference frame using the electrical rotor angle
\(\theta_e = P \cdot \theta_{\text{mech}}\) (where \(P\) is the motor
pole-pair count):

\[\begin{bmatrix} i_d \\ i_q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_e & \sin\theta_e \\ -\sin\theta_e & \cos\theta_e \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix}\]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Direct-Axis Current (\(i_d\)):} Aligns parallel with the rotor
  permanent magnet flux. Setting \(i_d^* = 0\) eliminates wasteful
  radial forces and maximizes electrical efficiency.
\item
  \textbf{Quadrature-Axis Current (\(i_q\)):} Aligns \(90^\circ\)
  electrical ahead of rotor flux, producing pure orthogonal
  electromagnetic torque:
\end{itemize}

\[\tau_{\text{motor}} = \frac{3}{2} P \lambda_{\text{pm}} i_q = K_t \cdot i_q\]

where \(\lambda_{\text{pm}}\) is the permanent magnet flux linkage
(\(\text{Wb}\)) and \(K_t\) is the motor torque constant
(\(\text{N}\cdot\text{m/A}\)).

\subsection*{Thermal Energy
Accumulator}\label{thermal-energy-accumulator}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Thermal Energy Accumulator}

To prevent motor stator insulation breakdown
(\(T > 155^\circ\text{C}\)), the motor driver integrates Joulean thermal
dissipation in real time:

\[E_{\text{thermal}}(t) = \int_0^t I_{\text{phase}}^2(\tau) R_{\text{stator}} \, d\tau\]

When \(E_{\text{thermal}}\) exceeds the continuous thermal rating
\(E_{\text{continuous}}\), the controller linearly derates peak torque
current
\(i_q^{\text{limit}} \leftarrow i_q^{\text{nominal}} \cdot \left(1 - \frac{T_j - 85^\circ\text{C}}{155^\circ\text{C} - 85^\circ\text{C}}\right)\).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\section*{6. Frequency-Domain Stability and Phase
Margin}\label{frequency-domain-stability-and-phase-margin}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{6. Frequency-Domain Stability and Phase
Margin}

\markright{6. Frequency-Domain Stability and Phase Margin}

In classical digital control, converting continuous commands to discrete
hardware outputs introduces uncompensated phase lag that erodes the
system's stability margin.

\subsection*{Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) Phase
Lag}\label{zero-order-hold-zoh-phase-lag}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{Zero-Order Hold (ZOH) Phase Lag}

A digital-to-analog converter holding a commanded setpoint constant over
sample period \(T\) is modeled by the Zero-Order Hold transfer function:

\[G_{\text{ZOH}}(s) = \frac{1 - e^{-sT}}{s}\]

Evaluating its frequency response \(s = j\omega\):

\[G_{\text{ZOH}}(j\omega) = T \cdot \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega T}{2}\right) e^{-j \frac{\omega T}{2}}\]

The magnitude attenuation is
\(\left| \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\omega T}{2}\right) \right|\), while the
\textbf{exact phase lag} is:

\[\Delta \phi_{\text{ZOH}} = -\frac{\omega T}{2} \quad (\text{radians}) = -\omega \cdot \frac{T}{2} \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} \quad (\text{degrees})\]

\subsection*{The Phase Margin Stability
Criterion}\label{the-phase-margin-stability-criterion}
\addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{The Phase Margin Stability Criterion}

Let \(\omega_c\) be the open-loop gain crossover frequency
(\(\|G(j\omega_c)\| = 1\)) of the physical mechanism, and
\(\text{PM}_{\text{nominal}}\) be the nominal phase margin. Total
sensorimotor transport delay
\(\tau_{\text{delay}} = \tau_{\text{compute}} + \frac{1}{2} T_{\text{sample}}\)
introduces phase lag:

\[\Delta \phi = -\omega_c \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}} \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\]

The effective closed-loop phase margin is:

\[\text{PM}_{\text{effective}} = \text{PM}_{\text{nominal}} - \omega_c \tau_{\text{delay}} \cdot \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\]

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Stability Limit:} If
  \(\tau_{\text{delay}} \ge \frac{\text{PM}_{\text{nominal}}}{\omega_c} \cdot \frac{\pi}{180^\circ}\),
  then \(\text{PM}_{\text{effective}} \le 0^\circ\). Stabilizing
  negative feedback flips into positive feedback, triggering explosive
  limit-cycle oscillations. As quantified in
  Table~\ref{tbl-math-phase-lag}, execution frequency directly dictates
  the preserved phase margin across operational cadences.
\end{itemize}
